lg.l: Poets, like cudgelled bullies, never do
At first or second blow submit to you;
But will provoke you still, and ne'er have done,
Till you are weary first with laying on.
The late so baffled scribbled of this day,
Though he stands trembling, bids me boldly say,
What we before most plays are used to do,
For poets out of fear first draw on you;
In a fierce prologue the still pit defy,
And ere you speak, like Castril, give the lie;
But though our Bayes's battle oft I've fought,
And with bruised knuckles their dear conquest bought,
Nay, never yet feared odds upon the stage,
In prologue dare not hector with the age,
But would take quarter from your saving hands,
Though Bayes within all yielding countermands,
Says you confed'rate wits no quarter give,
Therefor his play shan't ask your leave to live.
Well, let the vain rash fop, by huffing so,
Think to obtain the better terms of you;
But we, the actors, humbly with submit,
Now, and at any time, to a full pit.
Nay, often we anticipate your rage,
And murder poets for you, on our stage.
We set no guards upon our tiring-room,
But when with flying colours there you come,
We patiently you see, give up to you,
Our poets, virgin, nay our matrons too.

div2.head: SCENE ONE
div2.stage: Enter Horner, and Quack following him at a distance.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: [aside] A quack is a fit for a pimp as a midwife for a bawd; they are still but in their way both helpers of nature. – Well, my dear doctor, hast thou done what I desired?

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: I have undone you for ever with the women, and reported you throughout the whole town as bad as an eunuch, with as much trouble as if I had made you one in earnest.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But have you told all the midwives you know, the orange-wenches at the playhouses, the city husbands, and old fumbling keepers of this end of the town? For they'll be the readiest to report it.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: I have told all the chambermaids, waiting women, tire-women, and old women of my acquaintance; nay, and whispered it as a secret to 'em, and to the whisperers of Whitehall; so that you need not doubt 'twill spread, and you will be as odious to the handsome young women as –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: As the smallpox. Well –

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: And to the married women of this end of the town as –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: As the great ones, nay, as their own husbands.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: And to the city dames as aniseed Robin of filthy and contemptible memory; and they will frighten their children with your name, especially their females.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And cry, 'Horner's coming to carry you away.' I am only afraid 'twill not be believed. You told 'em 'twas by an English-French disaster, and an English-French chirurgeon, who has given me at once not only a cure but an antidote for the future against that damned malady, and that worse distemper, love, and all other women's evils?

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Your late journey into France has made it the more credible, and your being here a fortnight before you appeared in public looks as if you apprehended the shame, which I wonder you do not. Well, I have been hired by young gallants to belie 'em t'other way; but you are the first would be thought a man unfit for women.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Dear Mr Doctor, let vain rogues be contented only to be thought abler men than they are; generally 'tis all the pleasure they have. But mine lies another way.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: You take, methinks, a very preposterous way to it, and as ridiculous as if we operators in physic should put forth bills to disparage our medicaments, with hopes to gain customers.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Doctor, there are quacks in love as well as physic, who get but the fewer and worse patients for their boasting. A good name is seldom got by giving it oneself, and women no more than honour are compassed by bragging. Come, come, doctor, the wisest lawyer never discovers the merits of his cause till the trial; the wealthiest man conceals his riches, and the cunning gamester his play. Shy husbands and keepers like old rooks are not to be cheated, but by a new unpractised trick; false friendship will pass now no more than false dice upon 'em, no, not in the city.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: There are to ladies and a gentleman coming up.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: A pox! Some unbelieving sisters of my former acquaintance, who I am afraid expect their sense should be satisfied of the falsity of the report. No – this formal fool and women!

div2.stage: Enter Sir Jasper Fidget, Lady Fidget, and Mrs Dainty Fidget.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: His wife and sister.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: My coach breaking just now before your door, sir, I look upon as an occasional reprimand to me, sir, for not kissing your hands, sir, since your coming out of France, sir; and so my disaster, sir, has been my good fortune, sir; and this is my wife and sister, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What then, sir?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: My lady, and sister, sir. – Wife, this is Master Horner.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Master Horner, husband!

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: My lady, my Lady Fidget, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p:
Won't you be acquainted with her, sir? – [Aside] So the report is true, I find by his coldness or aversion to the sex; but I'll pay the wag with him.
(Aloud) Pray salute my wife, my lady, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I will kiss no man's wife, sir, for him, sir. I have taken my eternal leave, sir, of the sex already, sir,

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: [aside] Hah, hah, hah! I'll plague him yet. – Not know my wife, sir?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I do know your wife, sir, she's a woman, sir, and consequently a monster, sir, a greater monster than a husband, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: A husband! How, sir?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So, sir [makes horns]; but I make no more cuckolds, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Hah, hah, hah! Mercury, Mercury!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Pray, Sir Jasper, let us be gone from this rude fellow.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Who, by his breeding, would think he had ever been in France?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Foh! He's but too much a French fellow, such as hate women of quality and virtue for their love to their husbands, Sir Jasper; a woman is hated by 'em as much for loving her husband as for loving their money. But pray, let's be gone.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: You do well, madam, for I have nothing that you came for. I have brought over not so much as a bawdy picture, new postures, nor the second part of the Ecole des Filles, nor –

p.seg: Hold, for shame, sir! What d'y mean? You'll ruin yourself for ever with the sex.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Hah, hah, hah! He hates women perfectly, I find.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: What pity 'tis he should.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Ay, he's a base rude fellow for 't; but affectation makes not a woman more odious to them than virtue.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Because your virtue is your greatest affectation, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: How, you saucy fellow, would you wrong my honour?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: If I could.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: How d'y mean, sir?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Hah, hah, hah, no he can't wrong your ladyship's honour, upon my honour; he poor man - hark you in your ear – a mere eunuch –

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: O filthy French beast, soh, soh! Why do we stay? Let's be gone; I can't indure the sight of him.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Stay but till the chairs come; they'll be here presently.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Nor can I stay longer. 'Tis – let me see, a quarter and a half quarter of a minute past eleven; the Council will be sate, I must away. Business must be preferred always before love and ceremony with the wise, Mr Horner.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And the impotent, Sir Jasper.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, ay, the impotent, Master Horner, hah, ha ha!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: What, leave us with a filthy man alone in his lodgings!

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: He's an innocent man now, you know. Pray stay, I'll hasten the chairs to you. – Mr Horner, your servant; I should be glad to see you at my house. Pray come and dine with me, and play at cards with my wife after dinner; you are fit for women at that game yet, hah, ha! – [Aside] 'Tis as much a husband's prudence to provide innocent diversion for a wife as to hinder her unlawful pleasures, and he had better employ her than let her employ herself. – Farewell.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Your servant, Sir Jasper.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: I will not stay with him, foh!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, madam, I beseech you stay, if it be but to see I can be as civil to ladies yet as they would desire.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, no, foh, you cannot be civil to ladies.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: You as civil as ladies would desire?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, no, no! foh, foh, foh!

div2.stage: Exeunt Lady Fidget and Mrs Dainty.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Now I think I, or you yourself rather, have done your business with the women.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Thou art an ass. Don't you see, already upon the report and my carriage, this grave man of business leaves his wife in my lodgings, invites me to his house and wife, who before would not be acquainted with me out of jealousy?

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Nay, by this means you may be the more acquainted with the husbands, but the less with the wives.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Let me alone; if I can but abuse the husbands, I'll soon disabuse the wives. Stay – I'll reckon you up the advantages I am like to have by my stratagem. First, I shall be rid of all my old acquaintances, the most insatiable sorts of duns that invade our lodgings in a morning. And next to the pleasure of making a new mistress is that of being rid of an old one: and of all old debts, love, when it comes to be so, is paid the most unwillingly.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Well, you may be so rid of your old acquaintances, but how will you get any new ones?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Doctor, thou wilt never make a good chymist, thou art so incredulous and impatient. Ask but all the young fellows of the town if they do not lose more time, like huntsmen, in starting the game than in running it down; one knows not where to find 'em, who will, or will not. Women of quality are so civil you can hardly distinguish love from good breeding, and a man is often mistaken; but now I can be sure she that shews an aversion to me loves the sport, as those women that are gone, whom I warrant to be right. And then the next thing is your women of honour, as you call 'em, are only chary of their reputations, not their persons, and 'tis scandal they would avoid, not men. Now may I have, by the reputation of an eunuch, the privileges of one; and be seen in a lady's chamber in a morning as early as her husband; kiss virgins before their parents or lovers; and may be in short the passe partout of the town. Now, doctor.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Nay, now you shall be the doctor; and your process is so new that we do not know but it may succeed.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Not so new neither; probatum est, doctor.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Well, I wish you luck and many patients whilst I go to mine.

div2.stage: Enter Harcourt and Dorilant to Horner.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Come, your appearance at the play yesterday has, I hope, hardened you for the future against the women's contempt and the men's raillery, and now you'll abroad as you were wont?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Did I not bear it bravely?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: With a most theatrical impudence; nay, more than the orange-wenches shew there, or a drunken vizard-mask, or a great-bellied actress; nay, or the most impudent of creatures, an ill poet; or what is yet more impudent, a second-hand critic.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But what say the ladies? Have they no pity?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: What ladies? The vizard-masks, you know, never pity a man when all's gone, though in their service.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: And for the women in the boxes, you'd never pity them when 'twas in your power.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: They say 'tis pity but all that deal with common women should be served so.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Nay I dare swear, they won't admit you to play at cards with them, go to plays with 'em, or do the little duties which other shadows of men are wont to do for 'em.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Who do you call shadows of men?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Half-men.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What, boys?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Ay, your old boys, old beaux garçons, who, like superannuated stallions, are suffered to run, feed, and whinny with the mares as long as they live, though they can do nothing else.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, a pox on love and wenching! Women serve but to keep a man from better company; though I can't enjoy them, I shall you the more. Good fellowship and friendship are lasting, rational and manly pleasures.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: For all that, give me some of those pleasures you call effeminate too; they help to relish one another.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: They disturb one another.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, mistresses are like books; if you pore upon them too much, they doze you, and make you unfit for company, but if used discreetly, you are the fitter for conversation by 'em –

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: A mistress should be like a little country retreat near the town, not to dwell in constantly, but only for a night and away, to taste the town the better when a man returns.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I tell you, 'tis as hard to be a good fellow, a good friend and a lover of women as 'tis to be a good fellow, a good friend and a lover of money. You cannot follow both, then choose your side. Wine gives you liberty, love takes it away.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Gad, he's in the right on't.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Wine gives you joy, love grief and tortures, besides the chirurgeon's. Wine makes us witty, love only sots. Wine makes us sleep, love breaks it.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: By the world, he has reason, Harcourt.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Wine makes –

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Ay, wine makes us – makes us princes, love makes us beggars, poor rogues, ygad – and wine –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So, there's one converted. No, no, love and wine, oil and vinegar.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I grant it; love will still be uppermost.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Come, for my part I will have only those glorious, manly pleasures of being very drunk and very slovenly.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Mr Sparkish is below, sir.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: What, my dear friend? A rogue that is fond of me only, I think, for abusing him.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: No, he can no more think the men laugh at him than that women jilt him, his opinion of himself is so good.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, there's another pleasure by drinking, I thought not of; I shall lose his acquaintance, because he cannot drink; and you know 'tis a very hard thing to be rid of him, for he's one of those nauseous offerers at wit, who, like the worst fiddlers, run themselves into all companies.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: One that, by being in the company of men of sense, would pass for one.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And may so to the short-sighted world, as a false jewel amongst true ones is not discerned at a distance. His company is as troublesome to us as a cuckold's when you you have a mind to his wife's.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, the rogue will not let us enjoy one another, but ravishes our conversations, though he signifies no more to't than Sir Martin Mar-all's gaping, and aukerd thrumming upon the lute, does to his man's voice and music.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: And to pass for a wit in town, shews himself a fool every night to us, that are guilty of the plot.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Such wits as he are to a company of reasonable men, like rooks to the gamesters, who only fill a room at the table, but are so far from contributing to the play that they only serve to spoil the fancy of those that do.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Nay, they are used like rooks too, snubbed, checked and abused; yet the rogues will hang on.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: A pox on 'em, and all that force nature, and would be still what she forbids 'em! Affectation is her greatest monster.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Most men are the contraries to that they would seem. Your bully you see, is a coward with a long sword; the little humbly fawning physician with his ebony cane is he that destroys men.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: The usurer, a poor rogue possessed of mouldy bonds and mortgages; and we they call spendthrifts are only wealthy, who lay out his money upon daily new purchases of pleasure.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, your arrantest cheat is your trustee, or executor, your jealous man, the greatest cuckold, your church-man, the greatest atheist, and your noisy pert rogue of a wit, the greatest fop, dullest ass and worst company as you shall see, for here he comes.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How is't, sparks, how is't? Well, faith, Harry, I must rally thee a little, ha, ha, ha! upon the report in town of thee, ha, ha, ha! I can't hold i' faith; shall I speak?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Yes, but you'll be so bitter then.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Honest Dick and Frank here shall answer for me, I will not be extreme bitter, by the universe.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: We will be bound in ten thousand pound bond, he shall not be bitter at all.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Nor sharp, nor sweet.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What, not downright insipid?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay then, since you are so brisk and provoke me, take what follows. You must know, I was discoursing and rallying with some ladies yesterday, and they happened to talk of the fine new signs in town.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Very fine ladies I believe.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Said I, 'I know where the best new sign is.' 'Where?' says one of the ladies, 'In Covent Garden,' I replied. Said another, 'In what street?' 'In Russel Street,' answered I. 'Lord,' says another, 'I'm sure there was ne'er a fine new sign there yesterday.' 'Yes, but there was,' said I again, 'and it came out of France, and has been there a fortnight.'

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: A pox! I can hear no more, prithee.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, hear him out; let him tune his crowd a while.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: The worst music, the greatest preparation.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, faith, I'll make you laugh. 'It cannot be,' says a third lady. 'Yes, yes,' quoth I again. Says a fourth lady –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Look to't, we'll have no more ladies.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No? Then mark, mark, now. Said I to the fourth, 'did you never see Mr Horner? He lodges in Russel Street, and he's a sign of a man, you know, since he came out of France.' Heh, hah, he!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But the divel take me if thine be the sign of a jest.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: With that they all fell a-laughing till they bepissed themselves! What, but it does not move you, methinks? Well, I see one had as good go to law without a witness, as break a jest without a laughter on one's side, Come, come, sparks, but where do we dine? I have left at Whitehall an earl to dine with you.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Why, I thought thou hadst loved a man with a title better than a suit with a French trimming to't.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Go to him again.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, sir, a wit to me is the greatest title in the world.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But go dine with your earl, sir, he may be exceptious. We are your friends, and will not take it ill to be left, I do assure you.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Nay, faith, he shall go to him.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, pray, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: We'll thrust you out, if you wo'not. What, disappoint anybody for us?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, dear gentlemen, hear me.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, no, sir, by no means; pray go, sir.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Why, dear rogues –

div2.stage: They all thrust him out of the room.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: But, sparks, pray hear me. What, d'ye think I'll eat then with gay shallow fops and silent coxcombs? I think wit as necessary at dinner as a glass of good wine, and that's the reason I never have any stomach when I eat alone. Come, but where do we dine?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ev'n where you will.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: At Chateline's?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Yes, if you will.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Or at the Cock?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Yes, if you please.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Or at the Dog and Partridge?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, if you have mind to't, for we shall dine at neither.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw! With your fooling we shall lose the new play; and I would no more miss seeing a new play the first day than I would miss sitting in the wits' row. Therefore I'll go fetch my mistress and away.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Who have we here? Pinchwife?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Gentlemen, your humble servant.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, Jack, by thy long absence from the town, the grumness of thy countenance, and the slovenliness of thy habit, I should give thee joy, should I not, of marriage?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] Death, does he know I'm married too? I thought to have concealed it from him at least. – My long stay in the country will excuse my dress, and I have a suit of law, that brings me up to town, that puts me out of humour; besides, I must give Sparkish tomorrow five thousand pound to lie with my sister.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, you country gentlemen, rather than not purchase, will buy anything; and he is a cracked title, if we may quibble. Well, but am I to give thee joy? I heard thou wert married.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, the next thing that is to be heard is, thou'rt a cuckold.

p.seg: Insupportable name!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But I did not expect marriage from such a whoremaster as you, one that knew the town so much, and women so well.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, I have married no London wife.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Pshaw, that's all one; that grave circumspection in marrying a country wife is like refusing a deceitful pampered Smithfield jade, to go and be cheated by a friend in the country.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] A pox on him and his simile! – At least we are a little surer of the breed there, know what her keeping has been, whether foyled or unsound.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Come, come, I have known a clap gotten in Wales; and there are cousins, justices, clarks, and chaplains in the country, I won't say coach-men. But she's hansdome and young?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] I'll answer as I should do. – No, no, she has no beauty, but her youth; no attraction, but her modesty; wholesome, homely, and huswifely, that's all.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: He talks as like a grazier as he looks.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: She's too aukerd, ill-favoured, and silly to bring to town.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Then methinks you should bring her, to be taught breeding.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: To be taught? No, sir, I thank you, good wives and private soldiers should be ignorant. [Aside] I'll keep her from your instructions, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: The rogue is as jealous as if his wife were not ignorant.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, if she be ill-favoured, there will be less danger here for you than by leaving her in the country; we have such variety of dainties that we are seldom hungry.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: But they have always coarse, constant, swinging stomachs in the country.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Foul feeders indeed.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: And your hospitality is great there.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Open house, every man's welcome.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So, so, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But prithee, why wouldst thou marry her? If she be ugly, ill-bred and silly, she must be rich then.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: As rich as if she brought me twenty thousand pound out of this town; for she'll be as sure not to spend her moderate portion as a London baggage would be to spend hers, let it be what it would; so 'tis all one. Then, because she's ugly, she's the likelier to be my own; and being ill-bred, she'll hate conversation; and since silly and innocent, will not know the difference betwixt a man of one and twenty and one of forty.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nine – to my knowledge. But if she be silly, she'll expect as much from a man of forty-nine as from him of one and twenty. But methinks wit is more necessary than beauty, and I think no young woman ugly that has it, and no handsome woman agreeable without it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Tis my maxim, he's a fool that marries, but he's a greater that does not marry a fool. What is wit in a wife good for, but to make a man a cuckold?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Yes, to keep it from his knowledge.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: A fool cannot contrive to make her husband a cuckold.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, but she'll club with a man that can; and what is worse, if she cannot make her husband a cuckold, she'll make him jealous, and pass for one, and then 'tis all one.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, well, I'll take care for one, my wife shall make me no cuckold, though she had your help, Mr Horner; I understand the town, sir.

p.seg: His help!
He's come newly to town it seems, and has not heard how things are with him.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But tell me, has marriage cured thee of whoring, which it seldom does?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: 'Tis more than age can do.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, the word is, I'll marry and live honest; but a marriage vow is like a penitent gamester's oath, and ent'ring into bonds and penalties to stint himself to such a particular small sum at play for the future, which makes him but the more eager, and not being able to hold out, loses his money again, and his forfeit to boot.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Ay, ay, a gamester will be a gamester, whilst his money lasts; and a whoremaster whilst his vigour.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Nay, I have known 'em, when they are broke and can lose no more, keep a-fumbling with the box in their hands to fool with only, and hinder other gamesters.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: That had wherewithal to make lusty stakes.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, gentlemen, you may laugh at me, but you shall never lie with my wife; I know the town.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But prithee, was not the way you were in better? Is not keeping better than marriage?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: A pox on't, the jades would jilt me. I could never keep a whore to myself.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So then you only married to keep a whore to yourself? Well, but let me tell you, women, as you say, are like soldiers, made constant and loyal by good pay, rather than by oaths and covenants. Therefore I'd advise my friends to keep rather than marry, since too I find by your example it does not serve one's turn, for I saw you yesterday in the eighteen-penny place with a pretty country wench.

p.seg: How the divel did he see my wife then? I sate there that she might not be seen. But she shall never go to a play again.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What, dost thou blush at nine and forty, for having been seen with a wench?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: No, faith, I warrant 'twas his wife, which he seated there out of sight, for he's a cunning rogue, and understand the town.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: He blushes! Then 'twas his wife, for men are now more ashamed to be seen with them in public than with a wench.

p.seg: Hell and damnation! I'm undone, since Horner has seen her, and they know 'twas she.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But prithee, was it thy wife? She was exceedingly pretty; I was in love with her at that distance.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: You are like never to be nearer to her. Your servant, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, prithee, stay.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I cannot, I will not.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Come, you shall dine with us.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I have dine already.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Come, I know thou hast not. I'll treat thee, dear rogue, thou shalt spend none of thy Hampshire money today.

p.seg: Treat me! So he uses me already like his cuckold.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, you shall not go.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I must, I have business at home.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: To beat his wife. He's as jealous of her as a Cheapside husband of a Covent Garden wife.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, it is as hard to find an old whoremaster without jealousy and the gout, as a young one without fear or the pox.

lg.l: As gout in age from pox in youth proceedes,
So wenching past, then jealousy succeeds:
The worst disease that love and wenching breeds.

div2.head: SCENE ONE
div2.stage: Mrs Margery Pinchwife and Alithea: Mr Pinchwife peeping behind at the door.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray, sister, where are the best fields and woods to walk in in London?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: A pretty question! Why, sister, Mulberry Garden and St James's Park; and for close walks, the New Exchange.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray, sister, tell me why my husband looks so grum here in town, and keeps me up so close, and will not let me go a-walking, nor let me wear my best gown yesterday.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Oh, he's jealous, sister.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Jealous? What's that?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: He's afraid you should love another man.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: How should he be afraid of my loving another man, when he will not let me see any but himself?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Did he not carry you yesterday to a play?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, but we sate amongst ugly people. He would not let me come near the gentry, who sate under us, so that I could not see 'em. He told me none but naughty women sate there, whom they toused and moused; but I would have ventured for all that.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: But how did you like the play?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Indeed I was a-weary of the play, but I liked hugeously the actors; they are the goodliest properest men, sister!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Oh, but you must not like the actors, sister.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, how should I help it, sister? Pray, sister, when my husband comes in, will you ask leave for me to go a-walking?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p:
[aside] A-walking! Ha, ha! Lord, a country gentlewoman's leisure is the drudgery of a foot-post; and she requires as much airing as her husband's horses. Enter Mr Pinchwife to them.
But here comes your husband. I'll ask, though I'm sure he'll not grant it.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: He says he won't let me go abroad, for fear of catching the pox.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Fie! The smallpox, you should say.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh my dear, dear bud, welcome home! Why dost thou look so fropish? Who has nangered thee?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: You're a fool.

div2.stage: Mrs Pinchwife goes aside and cries.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Faith so she is, for crying for no fault, poor tender creature!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, you would have her as impudent as yourself, as errant a jilflirt, a gadder, a magpie, and to say all, a mere notorious town-woman?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Brother, you are my only censurer, and the honour of your family shall sooner suffer in your wife there than in me, though I take the innocent liberty of the town.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Hark you mistress, do not talk so before my wife. The innocent liberty of the town!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Why, pray, who boasts of any intrigue with me? What lampoon has made my name notorious? What ill women frequent my lodgings? I keep no company with any women of scandalous reputations.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, you keep the men of scandalous reputations company.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Where? Would you not have me civil? Answer 'em in a box at the plays, in the drawing-room at Whitehall, in St James's Park, Mulberry Garden, or –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Hold, hold! Do not teach my wife where the men are to be found. I believe she's the worse for your town documents already. I bid you keep her in ignorance as I do.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Indeed, be not angry with her bud, she will tell me nothing of the town, though I ask her a thousand times a day.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Then you are very inquisitive to know, I find?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Not I indeed, dear, I hate London. Our place-house in the country is worth a thousand of't. Would I were there again!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So you shall, I warrant. But were you not talking of plays and players when I came in? [To Alithea] You are her encourager in such discourses.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No indeed, dear, she chid me just now for liking the playermen.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] Nay, if she be so innocent as to own to me her liking them, there is no hurt in't. – Come my poor rogue, but thou likest none better than me?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes indeed, but I do, the playermen are finer folks.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But you love none better than me?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: You are mine own dear bud, and I know you. I hate a stranger.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, my dear, you must love me only, and not be like the naughty town-women, who only hate their husbands, and love every man else, love plays, visits, fine coaches, fine clothes, fiddles, balls, treats, and so lead a wicked town-life.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, if to enjoy all these things be a town-life, London is not so bad a place, dear.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: How! If you love me, you must hate London.

p.seg: The fool has forbid me discovering to her the pleasures of the town, and he is now setting her agog upon them himself.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But, husband, do the town-women love the player-men too?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Ay, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, you do not, I hope?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, no, bud, but why have we no player-men in the country?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ha! Mrs Minx, ask me no more to go to a play.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, why, love? I did not care for going; but when you forbid me, you make me, as't were, desire it.

p.seg: So 'twill be in other things, I warrant.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray, let me go to a play, dear.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Hold your peace, I wo'not.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, love?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, I'll tell you.

p.seg: Nay, if he tell her, she'll give him more cause to forbid her that place.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray, why, dear?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: First, you like the actors, and the gallants may like you.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, a homely country girl? No bud, nobody will like me.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I tell you yes, they may.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, no, you jest. I won't believe you, I will go.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I tell you then, that one of the lewdest fellows in town who saw you there, told me he was in love with you.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Indeed! Who, who, pray, who was't?

p.seg: I've gone too far, and slipped before I was aware. How overjoyed she is!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Was it any Hampshire gallant, any of our neighbours? I promise you, I am beholding to him.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I promise you, you lie; for he would but ruin you, as he has done hundreds. He has no other love for women but that such as he look upon women, like basilisks, but to destroy 'em.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, but if he loves me why should he ruin me? Answer me to that. Methinks he should not. I would do him no harm.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Hah, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
'Tis very well; but I'll keep him from doing you any harm, or me either. Enter Sparkish and Harcourt.
But here comes company; get you in, get you in.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But pray, husband, is he a pretty gentleman, that loves me?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
In baggage, in. [Thrusts her in: shuts the door.]
(aside) What, all the lewd libertines of the town brought to my lodging by this easy coxcomb! S'death, I'll not suffer it.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Here, Harcourt, do you approve my choice? Dear little rogue, I told you I'd bring you acquainted with all my friends, the wits, and –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, they shall know her as well as you yourself will, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: This is one of those, my pretty rogue, that are to dance at your wedding tomorrow; and him you must bid welcome ever, to what you and I have.

p.seg: Monstrous! –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Harcourt, how dost thou like her, faith? Nay, dear, do not look down; I should hate to have a wife of mine out of countenance at anything.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Wonderful!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Tell me, I say, Harcourt, how dost thou like her? Thou hast stared upon her enough to resolve me.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: So infinitely well that I could wish I had a mistress too, that might differ from her in nothing but her love and engagement to you.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Sir, Master Sparkish has often told me that his acquaintance were all wits and railleurs, and now I find it.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, by the universe, madam, he does not rally now; you may believe him. I do assure you, he is the honestest, worthiest, true-hearted gentleman – a man of such perfect honour, he would say nothing to a lady he does not mean.

p.seg: Praising another man to his mistress!

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Sir, you are so beyond expectation obliging that –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, egad, I am sure you do admire her extremely, I see't in your eyes. - He does admire you, madam. -By the world, don't you?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Yes, above the world, or the most glorious part of it, her whole sex; and till now I never thought I should have envied you or any man about to marry, but you have the best excuse for marriage I ever knew.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Nay, now sir, I'm satisfied you are of the society of the wits and railleurs, since you cannot spare your friend, even when he is but too civil to you; but the surest sign is, since you are an enemy to marriage, for that I hear you hate as much as business or bad wine.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Truly, madam, I never was an enemy to marriage till now, because marriage was never an enemy to me before.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: But why, sir, is marriage an enemy to you now? Because it robs you of your friend here? For you look upon a friend married as one gone into a monastery, that is, dead to the world.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: 'Tis indeed, because you marry him. I see madam, you can guess my meaning. I do confess heartily and openly I wish it were in my power to break the match, by heavens I would.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Poor Frank!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Would you be so unkind to me?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, no, 'tis not because I would be unkind to you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Poor Frank! No, egad, 'tis only his kindness to me.

p.seg: Great kindness to you indeed! Insensible fop, let a man make love to his wife to his face!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, dear Frank, for all my wife there that shall be, thou shalt enjoy me sometimes, dear rogue. By my honour, we men of wit condole for our deceased brother in marriage as much as for one dead in earnest. I think that was prettily said of me, ha, Harcourt? But come, Frank, be not melancholy for me.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, I assure you I am not melancholy for you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Prithee, Frank, dost think my wife that shall be there a fine person?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I could gaze upon her till I became as blind as you are.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How, as I am? How?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Because you are a lover, and true lovers are blind, stock blind.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: True, true. But by the world, she has wit too, as well as beauty. Go, go with her into a corner, and try if she has wit. Talk to her any thing, she's bashful before me.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Indeed, if a woman wants wit in a corner, she has it nowhere.

p.seg: Sir, you dispose of me a little before your time.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, nay, madam, let me have an earnest of your obedience, or – go, go, madam.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: How, sir, if you are not concerned for the honour of a wife, I am for that of a sister. He shall not debauch her. Be a pander to your own wife, bring men to her, let 'em make love before your face, thrust 'em into a corner together, then leave 'em in private! Is this your town wit and conduct?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Hah, ha, ha! A silly wise rogue would make one laugh more than a stark fool, hah, ha! I shall burst. Nay, you shall not disturb 'em; I'll vex thee, by the world.

div2.stage: Struggles with Pinchwife to keep him from Harcourt and Alithea.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: The writings are drawn, sir, settlements made; 'tis too late, sir, and past all revocation.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Then so is my death.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I would not be unjust to him.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Then why to me so?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I have no obligation to you.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: My love.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I had his before.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: You never had it; he wants, you see, jealousy, the only fallible sign of it.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Love proceeds from esteem; he cannot distrust my virtue. Besides, he loves me, or he would not marry me.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Marrying you is no more sign of his love than bribing your woman, that he may marry you, is a sign of his generosity. Marriage is rather a sign of interest than love; and he that marries a fortune covets a mistress, not loves her. But if you take marriage for a sign of love, take it from me immediately.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: No, now you have put a scruple in my head; but in short, sir, to end our dispute, I must marry him, my reputation would suffer in the world else.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, if you do marry him, with your pardon, madam, your reputation suffers in the world, and you would be thought in necessity for a cloak.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Nay, now you are rude, sir. – Mr Sparkish, pray come hither, your friend here is very troublesome, and very loving.

p.seg: Hold, hold!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: D'ye hear that?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Why, d'ye think I'll seem to be jealous, like a country bumpkin?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, rather be a cuckold, like a credulous cit.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Madam, you would not have been so little generous as to have told him.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Yes, since you could be so little generous as to wrong him.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Wrong him? No man can do't, he's beneath an injury. A bubble, a coward, a senseless idiot, a wretch so contemptible to all the world but you that –

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Hold, do not rail at him, for since he is like to be my husband, I am resolved to like him. Nay, I think I am obliged to tell him you are not his friend. – Master Sparkish, Master Sparkish.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: What, what? How, dear rogue, has not she wit?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: [speaks surlily] Not so much as I thought, and hoped she had.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Mr Sparkish, do you bring people to rail at you?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Madam –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How! No, but if he does rail at me, 'tis but in jest I warrant; what we wits do for one another, and never take any notice of it.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: He spoke so scurrilously of you, I had no patience to hear him; besides, he has been making love to me.

p.seg: True, damn'd tell-tale woman!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw, to shew his parts. We wits rail and make love often, but to shew our parts, as we have no affections, so we have no malice, we –

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: He said you were a wretch, below an injury.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw!

p.seg: Damned, senseless, impudent, virtuous jade! Well, since she won't let me have her, she'll do as good, she'll make me hate her.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: A common bubble.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: A coward.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw, pshaw!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: A senseless drivelling idiot.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How! Did he disparage my parts? Nay, then my honour's concern'd, I can't put up that, sir, by the world. Brother, help me to kill him. [Aside] I may draw now, since we have the odds of him. 'Tis a good occasion too, before my mistress –

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Hold, hold!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: What, what?

p.seg: I must not let 'em kill the gentleman neither, for his kindness to me; I am so far from hating him that I wish my gallant had his person and understanding. Nay, if my honour –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: I'll be thy death.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Hold, hold! Indeed, to tell the truth, the gentleman said after all that what he spoke was but out of friendship to you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How! Say, I am – I am a fool, that is, no wit, out of friendship to me?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Yes, to try whether I was concerned enough for you, and made love to me only to be satisfied of my virtue, for your sake.

p.seg: Kind, however –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, if it were so, my dear rogue, I ask thee pardon. But why would not you tell me so, faith?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Because I did not think on't, faith.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, Horner does not come; Harcourt, let's be gone to the new play. – Come, madam.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I will not go if you intend to leave me alone in the box and run into the pit, as you use to do.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw! I'lle leave Harcourt with you in the box to entertain you, and that's as good; if I sate in the box, I should be thought no judge, but of trimmings. – Come away Harcourt, lead her down.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, go thy ways for the flower of the true town fops, such as spend their estates before they come to 'em and are cuckolds before they're married. But let me go look to my own freehold. – How!

div2.stage: Enter My Lady Fidget, Mrs Dainty Fidget, and Mrs Squeamish.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Your servant, sir. Where is your lady? We are come to wait upon her to the new play.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: New play!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: And my husband will wait upon you presently.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] Damn your civility. Madam, by no means. I will not see Sir Jasper here till I have waited upon him at home; nor shall my wife see you till she has waited upon your ladyship at your lodgings.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Now we are here, sir –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, madam.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Pray let us see her.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: We will not stir till we see her.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
[aside] A pox on you all. – [Goes to the door, and returns.]
She has locked the door and is gone abroad.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, you have locked the door, and she's within.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: They told us below she was here.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: (aside) Will nothing do? Well it must out then. To tell you the truth, ladies, which I was afraid to let you know before lest it might endanger your lives, my wife has just now the smallpox come out upon her. Do not be frightened; but pray be gone ladies. You shall not stay here in danger of your lives. Pray get you gone ladies.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, no, we have all had 'em.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Alack, alack!

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Come, come, we must see how it goes with her. I understand the disease.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Come.

p.seg: Well, there is no being too hard for women at their own weapon, lying; therefore I'll quit the field.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Here's an example of jealousy.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Indeed, as the world goes, I wonder there are no more jealous, since wives are so neglected.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Pshaw! As the world goes, to what end should they be jealous?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Foh, 'tis a nasty world.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: That men of parts, great acquaintance, and quality should take up with, and spend themselves and fortunes in keeping little playhouse creatures, foh!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Nay, that women of understanding, great acquaintance, and good quality should fall a keeping too of little creatures, foh!

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Why, 'tis the men of quality's fault; they never visit women of honour and reputation, as they used to do; and have not so much as common civility for ladies of our rank, but use us with the same indifferency and ill breeding as if we were all married to 'em.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: She says true. 'Tis an errant shame women of quality should be so slighted. Methinks birth – birth should go for something. I have known men admired, courted, and followed for their titles only.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Ay, one would think men of honour should not love, no more than marry out of their own rank.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Fie, fie upom 'em! They are come to think cross breeding for themselves best, as well as for their dogs and horses.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: They are dogs and horses for't.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: One would think, if not for love, for vanity a little.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Nay, they do satisfy their vanity upon us sometimes, and are kind to us in their report; tell all the world they lie with us.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Damned rascals! That we should be only wronged by 'em; to report a man has had a person, when he has not had a person, is the greatest wrong in the whole world that can be done to a person.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Well, 'tis an arrant shame noble persons should be so wronged and neglected.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: But still 'tis an arranter shame for a noble person to neglet her own honour, and defame her own noble person with little inconsiderable fellows. Foh!

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: I suppose the crime against our honour is the same with a man of quality as with another.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: How! No, sure, the man of quality is likest one's husband, and therefore the fault should be the less.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: But then the pleasure should be the less.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Fie, fie, fie, for shame sister! Whither shall we ramble? Be continent in your discourse, or I shall hate you.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Besides, an intrigue is so much the more notorious for the man's quality.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: 'Tis true, nobody takes notice of a private man, and therefore with him 'tis more secret, and the crime's the less when 'tis not know.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: You say true. I'faith, I think you are in the right on't. 'Tis not an injury to a husband till it be an injury to our honours; so that a woman of honour loses no honour with a private person. And to say truth –

p.seg: So the little fellow is grown a private person with her.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: But still my dear, dear honour.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, my dear, dear of honour, thou hast still so much honour in thy mouth –

p.seg: That she has none elsewhere.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Oh, what d'ye mean to bring in these upon us?

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Foh! These are as bad as wits.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Foh!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Let us leave the room.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Stay, stay, 'faith, to tell you the naked truth –

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Fie, Sir Jasper! Do not use that word 'naked'.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Well, well, in short I have business at Whitehall, and cannot go to the play with you, therefore would have you go –

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: With those two to a play?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: No, not with t'other, but with Mr Horner. There can be no more scandal to go with him than with Mr Tattle, or Master Limberham.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: With that nasty fellow! No – no!

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Nay, prithee dear, hear me.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ladies –

div2.stage: [Horner, Dorilant, drawing near Squeamish and Dainty.]

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Stand off.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Do not approach us.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: You herd with the wits, you are obscenity all over.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And I would as soon look upon a picture of Adam and Eve, without fig leaves, as any of you, if I could help it; therefore keep off, and do not make us sick.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: What a divel are these?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, these are pretenders to honour, as critics to wit, only by censuring others; and as every raw, peevish, out-of-humoured, affected, dull, tea-drinking, arithmetical fop sets up for a wit by railing at men of sense, so these for honour, by railing at the Court, and ladies of as great honour as quality.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Come, Mr Horner, I must desire you to go with these ladies to the play, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I, sir!

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, ay, come, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I must beg your pardon, sir, and theirs, I will not be seen in women's company in public again for the world.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ha, ha! Strange aversion!

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: No, he's for women's company in private.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: He – poor man – he! Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: 'Tis a greater shame amongst lewd fellows to be seen in virtuous women's company than for the women to be seen with them.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Indeed, madam, the time was I only hated virtuous women, but now I hate the other too. I beg you pardon, ladies.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: You are very obliging, sir, because we would not be troubled with you.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: In sober sadness he shall go.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Nay, if he wo'not, I am ready to wait upon the ladies; and I think I am the fitter man.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: You, sir? No I thank you for that – Master Horner is a privileged man amongst the virtuous ladies; 'twill be a great while before you are so, heh, he, he! He's my wife's gallant, heh, he, he! No, pray, withdraw, sir, for as I take it, the virtuous ladies have no business with you.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: And I am sure he can have none with them. 'Tis strange a man can't come amongst virtuous women now but upon the same terms as men are admitted into the Great Turk's Seraglio. But heavens keep me from being an ombre player with 'em! But where is Pinchwife?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Come, come, man. What, avoid the sweet society of woman-kind? That sweet, soft, gentle, tame, noble creature woman, made for man's companion?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So is that soft, gentle, tame, and more noble creature a spaniel, and has all their tricks; can fawn, lie down, suffer beating, and fawn the more; barks at your friends when they come to see you, makes your bed hard, gives you fleas, and the mange sometimes. And all the difference is, the spaniel's the more faithful animal, and fawns but upon one master.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Heh, he, he!

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Oh, the rude beast!

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Insolent brute!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Brute! Stinking, mortified, rotten French wether, to dare –

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Hold, an't please your ladyship. For shame, Master Horner, your mother was a woman. [Aside] Now shall I never reconcile 'em. – Hark you, madam, take my advice in your anger. You know you often want one to make up your drolling pack of ombre players; and you may cheat him easily, for he's an ill gamester, and consequently loves play. Besides, you know, you have but two old civil gentlemen (with stinking breaths too) to wait upon you abroad; take in the third into your service. The other are but crazy. And a lady should have a supernumerary gentleman-usher, as a supernumerary coach-horse, lest sometimes you should be forced to stay at home.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: But are you sure he loves play, and has money?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: He loves play as much as you, and has money as much as I.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: The I am contented to make him pay for his scurrility. Money makes up in a measure all other wants in men. Those whom we cannot make hold for gallants, we make fine.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: [aside] So, so. Now to mollify, to wheedle him. – Master Horner, will you never keep civil company? Methinks 'tis time now, since you are only fit for them. Come, come, man, you must e'en fall to visiting our wives, eating at our tables, drinking tea with our virtuous relations after dinner, dealing cards to 'em, reading plays and gazettes to 'em, picking fleas out of their shocks for 'em, collecting receipts, new songs, women, pages, and footmen for 'em.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I hope they'll afford me better employment, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Heh, he, he! 'Tis fit you know your work before you come into your place. And since you are unprovided of a lady to flatter and a good house to eat at, pray frequent mine, and call my wife mistress, and she shall call you gallant, according to the custom.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Who, I?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Faith, thou shalt for my shake, come, for my sake only.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: For your sake –

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Come, come, (to ladies) here's a gamester for you, let him be a little familiar sometimes. Nay, what if a little rude? Gamesters may be rude with ladies, you know.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Yes, losing gamesters have a privilege with women.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I always thought the contrary, that the winning gamester had most privilege with women; for when you have lost your money to a man, you'll lose anything you have, all you have, they say, and he may use you as he pleases.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Heh, he, he! Well, win or lose, you shall have your liberty with her.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: As he behaves himself; and for your sake I'll give him admittance and freedom.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: All sorts of freedom, madam?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, ay, ay, all sorts of freedom thou canst take. And so go to her, begin thy new employment. Wheedle her, jest with her, and be better acquainted one with another.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Sister, what ails you? You are grown melancholy.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Would it not make anyone melancholy, to see you go every day fluttering about abroad, whilst I must stay at home like a poor, lonely, sullen bird in a cage?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Ay, sister, but you came young, and just from the nest to your cage, so that I thought you like it, and could be as cheerful in't as others that took their flight themselves early, and are hopping abroad in the open air.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, I confess I was quiet enough till my husband told me what pure lives the London ladies live abroad, with their dancing, meetings and junketings, and dressed every day in their best gowns; and I warrant you, play at ninepins every day of the week, so they do.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, what's here to do? You are putting the town pleasures in her head and setting her a-longing.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Yes, after nine pins. You suffer none to give her those longings you mean, but yourself.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I tell her of the vanities of the town like a confessor.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: A confessor! Just such a confessor as he that by forbidding a silly oastler to grease the horse's teeth, taught him to do't.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come Mistress Flippant, good precepts are lost when bad examples are still before us. The liberty you take abroad makes her hanker after it, and out of humour at home. Poor wretch! She desired not to come to London; I would bring her.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: She has been this week in town, and never desired, till this afternoon, to go abroad.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Was she not at a play yesterday?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, but she ne'er asked me. I was myself the cause of her going.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Then if she ask you again, you are the cause of her asking, and not my example.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, tomorrow night I shall be rid of you; and the next day before 'tis light, she and I'll be rid of the town, and my dreadful apprehensions. (To Mrs Pichwfe) Come, be not melancholy, for thou shalt go into the country after tomorrow, dearest.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Great comfort!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pish, what d'ye tell me of the country for?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: How's this! What, pish at the country?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let me alone, I am not well.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, if that be all. What ails my dearest?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Truly I don't know. But I have not been well since you told me there was a gallant at the play in love with me.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: That's by my example too!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, if you are not well, but are so concerned because a lewd fellow chanced to lie and say he liked you, you'll make me sick too.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Of what sickness?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, of that which is worse tan the plague, jealousy.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pish, you jeer. I'm sure there's no such disease in our receipt-book at home.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, thou never met'st with it, poor innocent – [Aside] Well, if thou cuckold me, 'twill be my own fault, for cuckolds and bastards are generally makers of their own fortune.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, but pray bud, let's go to a play tonight.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: (aside) 'Tis just done, she comes from it. (To Mrs Pinchwife) But why are you so eager to see a play?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Faith dear, not that I care one pin for their talk there. But I like to look upon the playermen, and would see, if I could, the gallant you say loves me. That's all, dear bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Is that all, dear bud?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: This proceeds from my example!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But if the play be done, let's go abroad however, dear bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, have a little patience, and thou shalt go into the country on Friday.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Therefore I would see first some sights, to tell my neighbours of. Nay, I will go abroad, that's once.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I'm the cause of this desire too.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But now I think on't, who was the cause of Horner's coming to my lodging today? That was you.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: No, you, because you would not let him see your handsome wife out of your lodging.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, O Lord! Did the gentleman come hither to see me indeed?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, no. You are not the cause of that damned question too, Mistress Alithea? – [Aside] Well, she's in the right of it. He is in love with my wife, and comes after her; 'tis so; but I'll nip his love in the bud, lest he should follow us into the country and break his chariot-wheel near our house, on purpose for an excuse to come to't. But I think I know the town.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, pray bud, let's go abroad before 'tis late; for I will go, that's flat and plain.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] So! The obstinacy already of a town-wife, and I must, whilst she's here, humour her like one. – Sister, how shall we do, that she may not be seen or known?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Let her put on her mask.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pshaw! A mask makes people but the more inquisitive, and is as ridiculous a disguise as a stage-beard; her shape, stature, habit will be known. And if we should meet with Horner, he would be sure to take acquaintance with us, must wish her joy, kiss her, talk to her, leer upon her, and the devil and all. No, I'll not use her to a mask, 'tis dangerous; for masks have made more cuckolds than the best faces that ever were known.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: How will you do then?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, shall we go? The Exchange will be shut, and I have a mind to see that.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So – I have it – I'll dress her up in the suit we are to carry down to her brother, little Sir James; nay, I understand the town tricks. Come, let's go dress her. A mask! No – a woman masked, like a covered dish, gives a man curiosity and appetite, when, it may be, uncovered, 'twould turn his stomach. No, no.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Indeed, your comparison is something a greasy one. But I had a gentle gallant used to say, a beauty masked, like the sun in eclipse, gathers together more gazers than if it shined out.

div2.head: SCENE TWO
div2.stage: The scene changes to the New Exchange. Enter Horner, Harcourt, Dorilant.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Engaged to women, and not sup with us?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, a pox on 'em all!

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: You were much a more reasonable man in the morning, and, had as noble resolutions against 'em as a widower of a week's liberty.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Did I ever think to see you keep company with women in vain?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: In vain! No – 'tis, since I can't love 'em, to be revenged on 'em.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Now your sting is gone, you looked in the box, amongst all those women, like a drone in the hive, all upon you; shoved and ill-used by 'em all, and thrust from one side to t'other.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Yet he must be buzzing amongst 'em still, like other old beetle-headed, liquorish drones. Avoid 'em, and hate'm as they hate you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Because I do hate 'em, and would hate 'em yet more, I'll frequent 'em. You may see by marriage, nothing makes a man hate a woman more than her constant conversation. In short, I converse with 'em, as you do with rich fools, to laugh at 'em and use 'em ill.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: But I would no more sup with women, unless I could lie with 'em, than sup with a rich coxcomb unless I could cheat him.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Yes, I had known thee sup with a fool for his drinking. If he could set out your hand that way only, you were satisfied, and if he were a wine-swallowing mouth 'twas enough.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Yes, a man drinks often with a fool, as he tosses with a marker, only to keep his hand in ure. But do the ladies drink?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Yes, sir, and I shall have the pleasure at least of laying 'em flat with a bottle, and bring as much scandal that way upon 'em as formerly t'other.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Perhaps you may prove as weak a brother amongst 'em that way as t'other.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Foh! Drinking with women is as unnatural as scolding with 'em; but 'tis a pleasure of decayed fornicators, and the basest way of quenching love.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Nay, 'tis drowning love instead of quenching it. But leave us for civil women too!

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Ay, when he can't be the better for 'em. We hardly pardon a man that leaves his friend for a wench, and that's a pretty lawful call.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Faith, I would not leave you for 'em, if they would not drink.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Who would disappoint his company at Lewis's for a gossiping?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Foh! Wine and women, good apart, together as nauseous as sack and sugar. But hark you, sir, before you go, a little of your advice; and old maimed general, when unfit for action, is fittest for counsel. I have other designs upon women than eating and drinking with them. I am in love with Sparkish's mistress, whom he is to marry tomorrow. Now how shall I get her?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, here comes one will help you to her.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: He! He, I tell you, is my rival, and will hinder my love.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, a foolish rival and a jealous husband assist their rival's designs; for they are sure to make their women hate them, which is the first step to their love for another man.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: But I cannot come near his mistress, but in his company.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Still the better for you, for fools are most easily cheated when they themselves are accessories. And he is to be bubbled of his mistress, as of his money, the common mistress, by keeping him company.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Who is that, that is to be bubbled? Faith let me snack, I han't met with a bubble since Christmas. Gad, I think bubbles are like their brother woodcocks, go out with the cold weather.

p.seg: A pox! He did not hear all, I hope.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, you bubbling rogues you, where do we sup? Oh, Harcourt, my mistress tells me you have been making fierce love to her all the play long, hah, ha! But I –

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I make love to her?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, I forgive thee; for I think I know thee, and I know her, but I am sure I know myself.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Did she tell you so? I see all women are like these of the Exchange, who, to enhance the price of their commodities, report to their fond customers offers which were never made 'em.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, women are as apt to tell before the intrigue as men after it, and so shew themselves the vainer sex. But hast thou a mistress, Sparkish? 'Tis as hard for me to believe it as that thou ever hadst a bubble, as you bragged just now.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Oh, you servant, sir; are you at your raillery sir? But we were some of us beforehand with you today at the play. The wits were something bold with you, sir. Did you not hear us laugh?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Yes, but I thought you had gone to plays to laugh at the poet's wit, not at your own.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Your servant, sir, no, I thank you. Gad, I go to a play as to a country treat, I carry my own wine to one, and my own wit to t'other, or else I'm sure I should not be merry at either. And the reason why we are so often louder than the players is because we think we speak more wit, and so become the poet's rival in his audience. For to tell you the truth, we hate the silly rogues. Nay, so much that we find fault even with their bawdy upon the stage, whilst we talk nothing else in the pit as loud.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But why shouldst thou hate the silly poets? Thou hast too much wit to be one, and they, like whores, are only hated by each other; and thou dost scorn writing, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Yes, I'd have you to know, I scorn writing. But women, women, that make men do all foolish things, make 'em write songs too; everybody does it. 'Tis even as common with lovers as playing with fans; and you can no more help rhyming to your Phyllis than drinking to your Phyllis.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Nay, poetry in love is no more to be avoided than jealousy.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: But the poets damned your songs, did they?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Damn the poets! They turned 'em into burlesque, as they call it. That burlesque is a hocus-pocus-trick they have got, which by the virtue of hictius doctius, topsey turvey they make a wise and witty man in the world a fool upon the stage you know not how. And 'tis before I hate 'em too, for I know not but it may be my own case; for they'll put a man into a play for looking a-squint. Their predecessors were contented to make serving-men only their stage fools, but these rogues must have gentlemen, with a pox to 'em, nay, knights. And indeed, you shall hardly see a fool upon the stage but he's a knight; and to tell you the truth, they have kept me these six years from being a knight in earnest, for fear of being knighted in a play, and dubbed a fool.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Blame 'em not; they must follow their copy, the age.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: But why shouldst thou be afraid of being in a play, who expose yourself every day in the playhouses, and as public places?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: 'Tis but being on the stage, instead of standing on a bench in the pit.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Don't you give money to painters to draw you like? And are you afraid of your pictures at length in a playhouse, where all your mistresses may see you?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: A pox! Painters don't draw the smallpox or pimples in one's face. Come, damn all your silly authors whatever, all books and booksellers, by the world, and all readers, courteous or uncourteous.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: But who comes here, Sparkish?

div2.stage: Enter Mr Pinchwife, and his wife in man's clothes, Alithea, Lucy her maid.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Oh hide me, there's my mistress too.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: She sees you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: But I will not see her. 'Tis time to go to Whitehall, and I must not fail the drawing-room.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Pray, first carry me, and reconcile me to her.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Another time. Faith, the King will have supped.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Not with the worse stomach for thy absence. Thou art one of those fools that think their attendance at the King's meals as necessary as his physicians', when you are more troublesome to him than his doctors or his dogs.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw! I know my interest, sir. Prithee hide me.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Your servant, Pinchwife. – What, he knows us not!

p.seg: Come along.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray, have you any ballads? Give me sixpenny worth.

sp.speaker: CLASP
sp.p: We have no ballads.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Then give me Covent Garden Drollery, and a play or two. – Oh, here's Tarugo's Wiles, and The Slighted Maiden, I'll have them.

p.seg: No, plays are not for your reading. Come along: will you discover yourself?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Who is that pretty youth with him, Sparkish?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: I believe his wife's brother, because he's something like her, but I never saw her but once.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Extremely handsome; I have seen a face like it too. Let us follow 'em.

div2.stage: Exeunt Pinchwife, Mrs Pinchwife, Alithea, Lucy; Horner, Dorilant following them.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Come, Sparkish, your mistress saw you and will be angry you go not to her. Besides, I would fain be reconciled to her, which none but you can do, dear friend.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Well, that's a better reason, dear friend. I would not go near her now for her's or my own sake, but I can deny you nothing. For though I have known thee a great while, never go if I do not love thee as well as a new acquaintance.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I am obliged to you indeed, dear friend. I would be well with her only to be well with thee still. For these ties to wives usually dissolve all ties to friends. I would be contented she should enjoy you a-nights, but I would have have you to myself a-days, as I have had, dear friend.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: And thou shalt enjoy me a-days, dear, dear friend, never stir; and I'll be divorced from her sooner than from thee. Come along.

p.seg: So, we are hard put to't when we make our rival our procurer. But neither she nor her brother would let me come near her now. When all's done, a rival is the best cloak to steal to a mistress under, without suspicion; and when we have once got to her as we desire, we throw him off like other cloaks.

div2.stage: Exit Sparkish, and Harcourt following him.
Re-enter Mr Pinchwife, Mrs Pinchwife in man's clothes.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
[To Alithea (offstage)] Sister, if you will not go, we must leave you. –
[Aside] The fool her gallant and she will muster up all the young saunterers of this place, and they will leave their dear seamstresses to follow us. What a swarm of cuckolds and cuckold-makers are here! Come, let't be gone, Mistress Margery.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Don't you believe that, I han't half my bellyful of sights yet.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Then walk this way.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Lord, what a power of brave signs are here! Stay – the Bull's Head, the Ram's Head, and the Stag's Head, dear –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, if every husband's proper sign here were visible, they would be all alike.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What d'ye mean by that, bud?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Tis no matter – no matter, bud.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray tell me; nay, I will know.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: They would be all bulls', stags', and rams' heads.

div2.stage: Re-enter Sparkish, Harcourt, Alithea, Lucy at t'other door.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, dear madam, for my sake you shall be reconciled to him.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: For your sake I hate him.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: That's something too cruel, madam, to hate me for his sake.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay indeed, madam, too, too cruel to me, to hate my friend for my sake.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I hate him because he is your enemy; and you ought to hate him too, for making love to me, if you love me.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: That's a good one! I hate a man for loving you! If he did love you, 'tis but what he can't help, and 'tis your fault not his, if he admires you. I hate a man for being of my opinion! I'll ne'er do't, by the world.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Is it for your honour or mine, to suffer a man to make love to me, who am to marry you tomorrow?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Is it for your honour or mine, to have me jealous? That he makes love to you is a sign you are handsome; and that I am not jealous is a sign you are virtuous. That, I think, is for your honour.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: But 'tis your honour too I am concerned for.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: But why, dearest madam, will you be more concerned for his honour than he is himself? Let his honour alone, for my sake and his. He, he has no honour –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How's that?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: But what my dear friend can guard himself.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Oho – that's right again.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
