sp.p: Your care of his honour argues his neglect of it, which is no honour to my dear friend here; therefore once more, let his honour go which way it will, dear madam.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay, ay, were it for my honour to marry a woman whose virtue I suspected, and could not trust her in a friend's hands?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Are you not afraid to lose me?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: He afraid to lose you, madam! No, no – you may see how the most estimable and most glorious creature in the world is valued by him. Will you not see it?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Right, honest Frank. I have that noble value for her that I cannot be jealous of her.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: You mistake him, he means you care not for me, nor who has me.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Lord, madam, I see you are jealous. Will you wrest a poor man's meaning from his words?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: You astonish me, sir, with your want of jealousy.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: And you make me giddy, madam, with your jealousy and fears, and virtue, and honour. Gad, I see virtue makes a woman as troublesome as a little reading or learning.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Monstrous!

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: [behind] Well, to see what easy husbands these women of quality can meet with; a poor chambermaid can never have such lady-like luck. Besides, he's thrown away upon her; she'll make no use of her fortune, her blessing; none to a gentleman for a pure cuckold, for it requires good breeding to be a cuckold.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I tell you then plainly, he pursues me to marry me.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw!

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Come, madam, you see you strive in vain to make him jealous of me. My dear friend is the kindest creature in the world to me.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Poor fellow.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: But his kindness only is not enough for me, without your favour. Your good opinion, dear madam, 'tis that must perfect my happiness. Good gentleman, he believes all I say; would you would do so. Jealous of me! I would not wrong him nor you for the world.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Look you there; hear him, hear him, and do not walk away so.

div2.stage: Alithea walks carelessly, to and fro.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I love you, madam, so –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How's that! Nay, now you begin to go too far indeed.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: So much I confess, I say I love you, that I would not have you miserable, and cast yourself away upon so unworthy and inconsiderable a thing as what you see here.

div2.stage: [Clapping his hand on his breast, points at Sparkish.]

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, faith, I believe thou wouldst not, now his meaning is plain. But I knew before thou wouldst not wrong me nor her.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, no, heavens forbid the glory of her sex should fall so low as into the embraces of such a contemptible wretch, the last of mankind – my dear friend here – I injure him.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, no, dear friend, I knew it. Madam, you see he will rather wrong himself than me, in giving himself such names.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Do not you understand him yet?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Yes, how modestly he speaks of himself, poor fellow.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Methinks he speaks impudently of yourself, since – before yourself too; insomuch that I can no longer suffer his scurrilous abusiveness to you, no more than his love to me.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, nay, madam, pray stay. His love to you! Lord, madam, has he not spoke yet plain enough?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Yes indeed, I should think so.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p:
Well then, by the world, a man can't speak civilly to a woman now, but presently she says he makes love to her. Nay, madam, you shall stay, with your pardon, since you have not yet understood him, till he has made an eclaircisment of his love to you, that is, what kind of love it is –
[To Harcourt] Answer to thy catechism, friend; do you love my mistress here?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Yes, I wish she would not doubt it.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: But how do you love her?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: With all my soul.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I thank him, methinks he speaks plain enough now.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: [to Alithea] You are out still. – But with what kind of love, Harcourt?

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: With the best and truest love in the world.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Look you there then, that is with no matrimonial love, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: How's that? Do you say matrimonial love is not best?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Gad, I went too far ere I was aware. But speak for thyself, Harcourt. You said you would not wrong me nor her.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: No, no, madam, e'en take him, for heaven's sake –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Look you there, madam.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Who should in all justice be yours, he that loves you most.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Look you there, Mr Sparkish, who's that?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Who should it be? Go on Harcourt.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Who loves you more than women titles, or fortune fools.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Look you there, he means me still, for he points at me.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Ridiculous!

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Who can only match your faith and constancy in love.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Who knows, if it be possible, how to value so much beauty and virtue.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Whose love can no more be equalled in the world than that heavenly form of yours.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Who could no more suffer a rival than your absence, and yet could no more suspect your virtue than his own constancy in his love to you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Who in fine loves you better than his eyes, that first made him love you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay – nay, madam, faith you shan't go till –

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Have a care, lest you make me stay too long.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: But till he has saluted you, that I may be assured you are friends, after his honest advice and declaration. Come, pray, madam, be friends with him.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: You must pardon me, sir, that I am not yet so obedient to you.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, invite your wife to kiss men? Monstrous! Are you not ashamed? I will never forgive you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Are you not ashamed that I should have more confidence in the chastity of your family than you have? You must not teach me; I am a man of honour, sir, though I am frank and free. I am frank, sir –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Very frank, sir, to share your wife with your friends.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: He is an humble, menial friend, such as reconciles the differences of the marriage bed. You know man and wife do not always agree. I design him for that use, therefore would have him well with my wife.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: A menial friend! You will get a great many menial friends by shewing your wife as you do.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: What then? It may be I have a pleasure in't, as I have to shew fine clothes at a playhouse the first day, and count money before poor rogues.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: He that shews his wife or money will be in danger of having them borrowed sometimes.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: I love to be envied, and would not marry a wife that I alone could love. Loving alone is as dull as eating alone. Is it not a frank age? And I am a frank person. And to tell you the truth, it may be I love to have rivals in a wife, they make her seem to a man still but as a kept mistress. And so good night, for I must to Whitehall. Madam, I hope you are now reconciled to my friend; amd so I wish you a good night, madam, and sleep if you can, for tomorrow you know I must visit you early with a canonical gentleman. Good night, dear Harcourt.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Madam, I hope you will not refuse my visit tomorrow, if it should be earlier, with a canonical gentleman, than Mr Sparkish's.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [coming between Alithea and Harcourt] This gentlewoman is yet under my care, therefore you must yet forbear your freedom with her, sir.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Must, sir?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, sir, she is my sister.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: 'Tis well she is, sir, for I must be her servant, sir. – Madam –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come away, sister, we had been gone, if it had not been for you, and so avoided these lewd rakehells, who seem to haunt us.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: How now, Pinchwife?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Your servant.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What! I see a little time in the country makes a man turn wild and unsociable, and only fit to converse with his horses, dogs, and his herds.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I have business, sir and must mind it; your business is pleasure, therefore you and I must go different ways.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, you may go on, but this pretty young gentleman –

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: The lady –

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: And the maid –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Shall stay with us, for I suppose their business is the same with ours, pleasure.

p.seg: 'Sdeath, he knows her, she carries it so sillily! Yet if he does not, I should be more silly to discover it first.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Pray, let us go, sir.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, come –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: [to Mrs Pinchwife] Had you not rather stay with us? Prithee, Pinchwife, who is this pretty young gentleman?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: One to whom I'm a guardian. [Aside] I wish I could keep her out of your hands –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Who is he? I never saw anything so pretty in all my life.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pshaw! Do not look upon him so much, he's a poor bashful youth; you'll put him out of countenance. Come away, brother.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Oh, your brother!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, my wife's brother. – Come, come she'll stay supper for us.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I thought so, for he is very like her I saw you at the play with, whom I told you I was in love with.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] O Jeminy! Is this he that was in love with me? I am glad on't I vow, for he's a curious fine gentleman, and I love him already too. [To Mr Pinchwife] Is this he, bud?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [to his wife] Come away, come away.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, what haste are you in? Why won't you let me talk with him?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Because you'll debauch him; he's yet young and innocent, and I would not have him debauched for any thing in the world. [Aside] How she gazes on him! The divel!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Harcourt, Dorilant, look you here, this is the likeness of that dowdy he told us of, his wife. Did you ever see a lovelier creature? The rogue has reason to be jealous of his wife, since she is like him, for she would make all that see her in love with her.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: And as I remember now, she is as like him here as can be.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: She is indeed very pretty, if she be like him.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Very pretty? A very pretty commendation! She is a glorious creature, beautiful beyond all things I ever beheld.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So, so.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: More beautiful than a poet's first mistress of imagination.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Or another man's last mistress of flesh and blood.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, now you jeer, sir. Pray don't jeer me.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, come. [Aside] By heavens, she'll discover herself.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I speak of your sister, sir.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, but saying she was handsome, if like him, made him blush. – [Aside] I am upon a wrack!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Methinks he is so handsome he should not be a man.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
(aside) Oh there, 'tis out, he has discovered her! I am not able to suffer any longer.
[To his wife] Come, come away, I say.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, by your leave, sir, he shall not go yet. –

div2.stage: [To them] Harcourt, Dorilant, let us torment this jealous rogue a little.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT and DORILANT
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I'll shew you.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, pray let him go, I cannot stay fooling any longer. I tell you his sister stays supper for us.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Does she? Come then we'll all go sup with her and thee.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, now I think on't, having stayed so long for us, I warrant she's gone to bed. – [Aside] I wish she and I were well out of their hands. – Come, I must rise early tomorrow, come.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well then, if she be gone to bed, I wish her and you a good night. Buy pray, young gentleman, present my humble service to her.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Thank you heartily, sir.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] S'death, she will discover herself yet in spite of me. – He is something more civil to you for your kindness to his sister than I am, it seems.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Tell her, dear sweet little gentleman for all your brother there, that you have revived the love I had for her at first sight in the playhouse.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But did you love her indeed, and indeed?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] So, so. – Away, I say.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, stay. Yes indeed, and indeed, pray do you tell her so, and give her this kiss for me.

p.seg: O heavens! What do I suffer! Now 'tis too plain he knows her, and yet –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And this, and this –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What do you kiss me for? I am no woman.

p.seg: So – there, 'tis out. Come, I cannot, nor will stay any longer.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, they shall send you lady a kiss too. Here Harcourt, Dorilant, will you not?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] How do I suffer this? Was I not accusing another just now for this rascally patience, in permitting his wife to be kissed before his face? Ten thousand ulcers gnaw away their lips! – Come, come.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p:
Good night, dear little gentleman. Madam, good night. Farewell Pinchwife.
[Apart to Harcourt and Dorilant] Did not I tell you I would raise his jealous gall?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So, they are gone at last. Stay, let me see first if the coach be at this door.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What, not gone yet? Will you be sure to do as I desired you, sweet sir?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Sweet sir, but what will you give me then?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Anything; come away into the next walk.

div2.stage: Exit Horner, haling away Mrs Pinchwife.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Hold, hold! What d'ye do?

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Stay, stay, hold –

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Hold, madam, hold! Let him present him, he'll come presently. Nay, I will never let you go till you answer my question.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: For God's sake, sir, I must follow 'em.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: No, I have something to present you with too, you san't follow them.

div2.stage: Alithea, Lucy, struggling with Harcourt and Dorilant.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Where? – how? – what's become of – gone! – whiter?

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: He's only gone with the gentleman, who will give him something, an't please your worship.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Something! – give him something, with a pox! Where are they?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: In the next walk only, brother.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Only, only! Where, where?

div2.stage: Exit Pinchwife, and returns presently, then goes out again.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: What's the matter with him? Why so much concerned? But dearest madam –

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Pray let me go, sir, I have said and suffered enough already.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Then you will not look upon, not pity my sufferings?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: To look upon 'em when I cannot help 'em, were cruelty, not pity; therefore I will never see you more.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Let me then, madam, have my privilege of a banished lover, complaining or railing, and giving you but a farewell reason why, if you cannot condescend to marry me, you should not take that wretch my rival.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: He only, not you, since my honour is engaged so far to him, can give a reason why I should not marry him; but if he be true, and what I think him to me, I must be so to him. Your servant, sir.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Have women only constancy when 'tis a vice, and like fortune only true to fools?

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: [To Lucy, who struggles to get from him] Thou shalt not stir, thou robust creature. You see I can deal with you, therefore you should stay the rather, and be kind.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Gone, gone, not to be found! Quite gone! Ten thousand plagues go with 'em! Which way went they?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: But into t'other walk, brother.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Their business will be done presently, sure, an't please your worship; it can't be long in doing, I'm sure on't.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Are they not there?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, you know where they are, you infamous wretch, eternal shame of your family, which you do not dishonour enough yourself, you think, but you must help her to do it too, thou legion of bawds!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Good brother –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Damned, damned sister!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Look you here, she's coming.

div2.stage: Enter Mrs Pinchwife in man's clothes, running with her hat under her arm, full of oranges and dried fruit, Horner following.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O dear bud, look you here what I have got, see!

p.seg: And what I have got here, too, which you can't see.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: The fine gentleman has given me better things yet.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Has he so? – [Aside] Out of breath and coloured! I must hold yet.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I have only given your little brother an orange, sir.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
[to Horner] Thank you, sir.
[Aside] You have only squeezed my orange, I suppose, and given it me again; yet I must have a city patience.
[To his wife] Come, come away.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Stay till I have put up my fine things, bud.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: O Master Horner, come, come, the ladies stay for you. Your mistress, my wife, wonders you make not more haste to her.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I have stayed this half hour for you here, and 'tis your fault I am not now with your wife.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: But pray, don't let her know so much. The truth on't is, I was advancing a certain project to his Majesty, about – I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, let's go, and hear it at your house. – Good night, sweet little gentleman. One kiss more; you'll remember me now, I hope.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: What, Sir Jasper, will you separate friends? He promised to sup with us; and if you take him to your house, you'll be in danger of our company too.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Alas, gentleman, my house is not fit for you. There are none but civil women there, which are not for your turn. He, you know, can bear with the society of civil women now, ha, ha, ha! Besides, he's one of my family – he's – heh, heh, heh!

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: What is he?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Faith, my eunuch, since you'll have it, heh, he, he!

div2.stage: Exit Sir Jasper Fidget and Horner.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: I rather wish thou wert his, or my cuckold. Harcourt, what a good cuckold is lost there for want of a man to make him one! Thee and I cannot have Horner's privilege, who can make use of it.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Ay, to poor Horner 'tis like coming to an estate at three-score, when a man can't be the better for 't.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Presently, bud.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Come, let us go too. [To Alithea] Madam, your servant. [To Lucy] Good night, strapper.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Madam, though you will not let me have a good day or night, I wish you one; but dare not name the other half of my wish.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Good night, sir, for ever.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I don't know where to put this here, dear bud, you shall eat it. Nay, you shall have part of the fine gentleman's good things, or treat as you call it, when we come home.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Indeed I deserve it, since I furnished the best part of it.

lg.l: The gallant treats, presents, and gives the ball;
But 'tis the absent cuckold pays for all.

div2.head: SCENE ONE
div2.stage: In Pinchwife's house in the morning.
Lucy, Alithea dressed in new clothes.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Well madam, now have I dressed you, and set you out with so many ornaments, and spent upon you ounces of essence and pulvilio; and all this for no other purpose but as people adorn and perfume a corpse for a stinking second-hand grave; such or as bad I think Master Sparkish's bed.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Hold your peace!

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Nay, madam, I will ask you the reason why you would banish poor Master Harcourt for ever from your sight. How could you be so hard-hearted?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: 'Twas because I was not hard-hearted.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: No, no. 'Twas stark love and kindness, I warrant.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: It was so. I would see him no more because I love him.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Hey-day, a very pretty reason!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: You do not understand me.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: I wish you may yourself.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I was engaged to marry, you see, another man, whom my justice will not suffer me to deceive or injure.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Can there be a greater cheat or wrong done to a man than to give him your person without your heart? I should make a conscience of it.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I'll retrieve it for him after I am married a-while.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: The woman that marries to love better will be as much mistaken as the wencher that marries to live better. No, madam, marrying to increase love is like gaming to become rich; alas, you only lose what little stock you had before.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I find by your rhetoric you have been bribed to betray me.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Only by his merit, that has bribed your heart, you see, against your word and rigid honour. But what a divel is this honour? 'Tis sure a disease in the head, like the megrim, or falling sickness, that always hurries people away to do themselves mischief. Men lose their lives by it; women what's dearer to 'em, their love, the life of life.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Come, pray talk you no more of honour, nor Master Harcourt. I wish the other would come to secure my fidelity to him, and his right in me.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: You will marry him then?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Certainly. I have given him already my word, and will my hand too, to make it good, when he comes.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Well, I wish I may never stick pin more if he be not an arrant natural to t'other fine gentleman.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I own he wants the wit of Harcourt, which I will dispense withal, for another want he has, which is want of jealousy, which men of wit seldom want.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Lord, madam, what should you do with a fool to your husband? You intend to be honest, don't you? Then that husbandly virtue, credulity, is thrown away upon you.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: He only that could suspect my virtue should have cause to do it; 'tis Sparkish's confidence in my truth that obliges me to be so faithful to him.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: You are not sure his opinion may last.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I am satisfied 'tis impossible for him to be jealous after the proofs I have had of him. Jealousy in a husband – heaven defend me from it! It begets a thousand plagues to a poor woman, the loss of her honour, her quiet, and her –

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: And her pleasure.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: What d'ye mean, impertinent?

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Liberty is a great pleasure, madam.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I say loss of her honour, her quiet, nay, her life sometimes; and what's as bad almost, the loss of this town. That is, she is sent into the country, which is the last ill usage of a husband to a wife, I think.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: [aside] Oh, does the wind lie there? – Then of necessity, madam, you think a man must carry his wife into the country, if he be wise. The country is as terrible, I find, to our young English ladies as a monastery to those abroad. And on my virginity, I think they would rather marry a London gaoler than a High Sheriff of a country, since neither can stir from his employment. Formerly women of wit married fools for a great estate, a fine seat, or the like; but now 'tis for a pretty seat only in Lincoln's Inn fields, St James's fields, or the Pall Mall.

div2.stage: Enter to them Sparkish, and Harcourt dressed like a parson.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Madam, your humble servant, a happy day to you, and to us all.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Who have we here?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: My chaplain, faith. O madam, poor Harcourt remembers his humble service to you; and in obedience to your last commands, refrains coming into your sight.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Is not that he?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, fie, no; but to shew that he ne'er intended to hinder our match, has sent his brother here to join our hands. When I get me a wife, I must get her a chaplain, according to the custom; this is his brother, and my chaplain.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: His brother?

p.seg: And your chaplain, to preach in your pulpit then.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: His brother!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, I knew you would not believe it. – I told you, sir, she would take you for your brother Frank.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Believe it!

p.seg: His brother! Hah, ha, he! He has a trick left still, it seems.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, my dearest, pray let us go to church before the canonical hour is past.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: For shame, you are abused still.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: By the world, 'tis strange now you are so incredulous.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: 'Tis strange you are so credulous.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Dearest of my life, hear me. I tell you this is Ned Harcourt of Cambridge, by the world; you see he has a sneaking college look. 'Tis true he's something like his brother Frank, and they differ from each other no more than in their age, for they were twins.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Hah, ha, he!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Your servant, sir, I cannot be so deceived, though you are. But come, let's hear, how do you know what you affirm so confidently?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Why, I'll tell you all. Frank Harcourt coming to me this morning, to wish me joy and present his service to you, I asked him if he could help me to a parson; whereupon he told me he had a brother in town who was in orders, and he went straight away and sent him you see there to me.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Yes, Frank goes and puts on a black-coat, then tells you he is Ned. That's all you have for't.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw, pshaw! I tell you by the same token the midwife put her garter about Frank's neck to know 'em asunder, they were so like.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Frank tells you this too.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay, and Ned there too; nay, they are both in a story.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: So, so. Very foolish!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Lord if you won't believe one, you had best try him by your chambermaid there, for chambermaids must needs know chaplains from other men, they are so used to 'em.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Let's see. Nay, I'll be sworn he has the canonical smirk, and the filthy, clammy palm of a chaplain.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Well, most reverend doctor, pray let us make an end of this fooling.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: With all my soul, divine, heavenly creature, when you please.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: He speaks like a chaplain indeed.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Why, was there not 'soul', 'divine', 'heavenly', in what he said?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Once more, most impertinent black-coat, cease your persecution, and let us have a conclusion of this ridiculous love.

p.seg: I had forgot. I must suit my style to my coat, or I wear it in vain.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I have no more patience left. Let us make once an end of this troublesome love, I say.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: So be it, seraphic lady, when your honour shall think it meet and convenient so to do.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Gad, I'm sure none but a chaplain could speak so, I think.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Let me tell you, sir, this dull trick will not serve your turn; though you delay our marriage, you shall not hinder it.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Far be it from me, munificent patroness, to delay your marriage. I desire nothing more than to marry you presently, which I might do, if you yourself would; for my noble, good-natured and thrice-generous patron here would not hinder it.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, poor man, not I, faith.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: And now, madam, let me tell you plainly, nobody else shall marry you. By heavens, I'll die first, for I'm sure I should die after it.

p.seg: How his love has made him forget his function, as I have seen it in real parsons.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: That was spoken like a chaplain too. – Now you understand him, I hope.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Poor man, he takes it heinously to be refused. I can't blame him, 'tis putting an indignity upon him not to be suffered. But you'll pardon me madam, it shan't be; he shall marry us. Come away, pray, madam.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Hah, ha, he! More ado! 'Tis late.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Invincible stupidity! I tell you he would marry me as your rival, not as your chaplain.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: [pulling her away] Come, come, madam.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: I pray madam, do not refuse this reverend divine the honour and satisfaction of marrying you; for I dare say he has set his heart upon't, good doctor.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: (to Harcourt) What can you hope or design by this?

p.seg: I could answer her, a reprieve for a day only often revokes a hasty doom. At worst, if she will not take mercy on me and let me marry her, I have at least the lover's second pleasure, hind'ring my rival's enjoyment, though but for a time.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, madam, 'tis e'en twelve a clock, and my mother charged me never to be married out of the canonical hours. Come, come, Lord, here's such a deal of modesty, I warrant, the first day.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Yes, an't please your worship, married women shew all their modesty the first day, because married men shew all their love the first day.

div2.stage: Exeunt Sparkish, Alithea, Harcourt, and Lucy.

div2.head: SCENE TWO
div2.stage: The scene changes to a bedchamber, where appear Pinchwife, Mrs Pinchwife.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, tell me, I say.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Lord, han't I told it an hundred times over?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] I would try if, in the repetition of the ungrateful tale, I could find her altering it in the least circumstance, for if her story be false, she is so too. – Come, how was't, baggage?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Lord, what pleasure you take to hear it, sure!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, you take more in telling it I find. But speak, how was't?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: He carried me up into the house next to the Exchange.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So; and you two were only in the room?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, for he sent away a youth that was there for some dried fruit and China oranges.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Did he so? Damn him for it – and for –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But presently came up the gentlewoman of the house.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, 'twas well she said. But what did he do whilst the fruit came?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: He kissed me an hundred times, and told me he fancied he kissed my fine sister, meaning me you know, whom he said he loved with all his soul, and bid me be sure to tell her so, and to desire her to be at her window by eleven of the clock this morning, and he would walk under it at that time.

p.seg: And he was as good as his word, very punctual, a pox reward him for't.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, and he said if you were not within, he would come up to her, meaning me you kow, bud, still.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So. – [Aside] He knew her certainly, but for this confession, I am obliged to her simplicity. – But what, you stood very still when he kissed you?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, I warrant you; would you have had me discovered myself?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But you told me he did some beastliness to you, as you called it. What was't?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, he put –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why he put the tip of his tongue between my lips, and so musled me. And I said I'd bite it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: An eternal canker seize it, for a dog!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, you need not be so angry with him neither, for to say truth, he has the sweetest breath I ever knew.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: The devil! – You were satisfied with it then, and would do it again?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Not unless he should force me.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Force you, changeling! I tell you no woman can be forced.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, but she may sure, by such a one as he, for he's a proper, goodly strong man. 'Tis hard, let me tell you, to resist him.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: (aside) So, 'tis plain she loves him, yet she has not love enough to make her conceal it from me; but the sight of him will increase her aversion for me, and love for him, and that love instruct her how to deceive me, and satisfy him, all idiot as she is. Love! 'Twas he gave women first their craft, their art of deluding. Out of nature's hands they came plain, open, silly and fit for slaves, as she and Heaven intended 'em; but damned love – well, I must strangle that little monster whilst I can deal with him. (To her) Go, fetch pen, ink and paper out of the next room.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
[aside] Why should women have more invention in love than men? It can only be because they have more desires, more soliciting passions, more lust, and more of the devil. Mrs Pinchwife returns.
Come, minx, sit down and write.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, dear bud, but I can't do't very well.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I wish you could not at all.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But what should I write for?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I'll have you write a letter to your lover.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O Lord, to the fine gentleman, a letter!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, to the fine gentleman.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Lord, you do but jeer; sure you jest.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I am not so merry. Come, write as I bid you.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, do you think I am a fool?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] She's afraid I would not dictate any love to him, therefore she's unwilling. – But you had best begin.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Indeed, and indeed, but I won't, so I won't.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Because he's in town; you may send for him if you will.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Very well, you would have him brought to you. Is it come to this? I say take the pen and write, or you'll provoke me.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Lord, what d'ye make a fool of me for? Don't I know that letters are never writ but from the country to London, and from London into the country? Now he's in town, and I am in town too; therefore I can't write to him, you know.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] So; I am glad it is no worse, she is innocent enough, yet – Yes, you may, when your husband bids you, write letters to people that are in town.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, may I so? Then I'm satisfied.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, begin. [Dictates] 'Sir' –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Shan't I say, 'Dear Sir'? – You know one says always something more than bare 'Sir'.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Write as I bid you, or I will write whore with this penknife in your face.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
Nay, good bud.
[She writes] 'Sir' –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Though I suffered last night your nauseous, loathed kisses and embraces.' – Write.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, why should I say so? You know I told you he had a sweet breath.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Write!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let me but put out 'loathed'.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Write, I say!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well then.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let's see what have you writ. [Takes the paper, and reads.] 'Though I suffered last night your kisses and embraces'. – Thou impudent creature, where is 'nauseous' and 'loathed'?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I can't abide to write such filthy words.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
Once more, write as I'd have you and question it not, or I will spoil thy writing with this.
[Holds up the penknife.] I will stab out those eyes that cause my mischief.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O Lord, I will!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So – so. – Let's see now! [Reads] 'Though I suffered last night your nauseous, loathed kisses and embraces' – go on – 'yet I would not have you presume that you shall ever repeat them.' – So.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I have writ it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: On then, - 'I then concealed myself from your knowledge to avoid your insolencies' –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'The same reason, now I am out of your hands' –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Makes me own to you my unfortunate, though innocent frolick, of being in man's clothes.'

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'That you may for ever more cease to pursue her, who hates and detests you' –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So – h –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, do you sigh? – 'detests you – as much as she loves her husband and her honour'.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I vow, husband, he'll ne'er believe I should write such a letter.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, he'd expect a kinder from you? Come now, your name only.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, shan't I say 'Your most faithful, humble servant till death'?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, tormenting fiend! – [Aside] Her style, I find, would be very soft. – Come, wrap it up now, whilst I go fetch wax and a candle; and write on the back side, 'For Mr Horner'.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
'For Mr Horner'. – So, I am glad he has told me his name. Dear Mr Horner! But why should I send thee such a letter that will vex thee, and make thee angry with me? – Well, I will not send it. – Ay, but then my husband will kill me, for I see plainly he won't let me love Mr Horner – but what care I for my husband? – I won't, so I won't, send poor Mr Horner such a letter – but then my husband – But oh – what if I writ at bottom my husband made me write it? – Ay, but then my husband would see't. – Can one have no shift? Ah, a London woman would have had a hundred presently. Stay – what if I should write a letter, and wrap it up like this, and write on't too? Ay, but then my husband would see't. – I don't know what to do. – But yet y'vads, I'll try, so I will – for I will not send this letter to poor Mr Horner, come what will on't. [She writes, and repeats what she hath writ.]
'Dear, sweet Mr Horner' – so – 'my husband would have me send you a base, rude, unmannerly letter – but I won't – so – 'and would have me forbid you loving me – but I won't' – so – 'and would have me say to you I hate you, poor Mr Horner – but I won't tell a lie for him' – there – 'for I'm sure if you and I were in the country at cards together', – so – 'I could not help treading on your toe under the table' – so – 'or rubbing knees with you, and staring in your face till you saw me' – very well – 'and then looking down, and blushing for an hour together' – so – 'but I must make haste before my husband come; and now he has taught me to write letters, you shall have longer ones from me, who am
Dear, dear, poor dear Mr Horner, your most humble friend, and servant to command 'till death,
Margery Pinchwife.'
Stay, I must give him a hint at bottom – so – now wrap it up just like t'other – so – now write 'For Mr Horner'. – But oh now what shall I do with it? For here comes my husband.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] I have been detained by a sparkish coxcomb who pretended a visit to me; but I fear 'twas to my wife. – What, have you done?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, ay bud, just now.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let's see. What d'ye tremble for? What, you would not have it go?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Here. – [Aside] No, I must not give him that; so I had been served if I had given him this.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [he opens, and reads the first letter] Come, where's the wax and seal?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] Lord, what shall I do now? Nay then I have it. – Pray let me see't. Lord you think me so arrant a fool I cannot seal a letter; I will do't, so I will.

div2.stage: Snatches the letter from him, changes it for the other, seals it, and delivers it to him.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, I believe you will learn that, and other things too, which I would not have you.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: So, han't I done it curiously? [Aside] I think I have; there's my letter going to Mr Horner; since he'll needs have me send letters to folks.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Tis very well, but I warrant you would not have it go now?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes indeed, but I would, bud – now.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
Well, you are a good girl then. Come, let me lock you up in your chamber till I come back; and be sure you come not within three strides of the window when I am gone, for I have a spy in the street. Exit Mrs Pinchwife. Pinchwife locks the door.
At least, 'tis fit she think so. If we do not cheat women, they'll cheat us; and fraud may be justly used with secret enemies, of which a wife is the most dangerous; and he that has a handsome one to keep, and a frontier town, must provide against treachery rather than open force. Now I have secured all within, I'll deal with the foe without with false intelligence.

div2.head: SCENE THREE
div2.stage: The scene changes to Horner's lodging.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Well sir, how fadges the new design? Have you not the luck of all your brother projectors, to deceive only yourself at last?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, good domine doctor, I deceive you it seems, and others too; for the grave matrons and old rigid husbands think me as unfit for love as they are; but their wives, sisters and daughters know, some of 'em, better things already.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Already!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Already, I say. Last night I was drunk with half a dozen of your civil persons, as you call 'em, and people of honour, and so was made free of their society and dressing-rooms for ever hereafter; and am already come to the privileges of sleeping upon their pallets, warming smocks, tying shoes and garters and the like, doctor – already, already doctor.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: You have made use of your time, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I tell thee, I am now no more interruption to 'em, when they sing or talk bawdy, than a little squab French page, who speaks no English.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: But do civil persons and women of honour drink and sing bawdy songs?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Oh, amongst friends, amongst friends. For your bigots in honour are just like those in religion; they fear the eye of the world more than the eye of Heaven; and think there is no virtue but railing at vice, and no sin but giving scandal. They rail at a poor little kept player, and keep themselves some young, modest, pulpit comedian to be privy to their sins in their closets, not to tell 'em of them in their chapels.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Nay, the truth on't is, priests amongst the women now have quite got the better of us lay confessors, physicians.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p:
And they are rather their patients, but – Enter My Lady Fidget, looking about her.
Now we talk of women of honour, here comes one. Step behind the screen there, and but observe if I have not particular privileges with the women of reputation already, doctor, already.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Well, Horner, am not I a woman of honour? You see, I'm as good as my word.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And you shall see madam, I'll not be behindhand with you in honour; and I'll be as good as my word too, if you please but to withdraw into the next room.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: But first, my dear sir, you must promise to have care of my dear honour.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: If you talk a word more of your honour, you'll make me incapable to wrong it. To talk of honour in the mysteries of love is like talking of Heaven or the Deity in an operation of witchcraft, just when you are employing the devil; it makes the charm impotent.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Nay, fie, let us not be smooty. But you talk of mysteries and bewitching to me; I don't understand you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I tell you madam, the word 'money' in a mistress's mouth at such a nick of time is not a more disheart'ning sound to a younger brother than of honour to an eager lover like myself.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: But you can't blame a lady of my reputation to be chary.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Chary! I have been chary of it already, by the report I have caused of myself.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Ay, but if you should ever let other women know that dear secret, it would come out. Nay, you must have a great care of your conduct; for my acquaintance are so censorious – oh 'tis a wicked, censorious world, Mr Horner! – I say, are so censorious and detracting that perhaps they'll talk to the prejudice of my honour, though you should not let them know the dear secret.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, madam, rather than they shall prejudice your honour, I'll prejudice theirs; and to serve you, I'll lie with 'em all, make the secret their own, and then they'll keep it. I am a Machiavel in love, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Oh no sir, not that way!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, the devil take me if censorious women are to be silenced any other way.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: A secret is better kept, I hope, by a single person than a multitude; therefore pray do not trust anybody else with it, dear, dear Mr Horner.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: How now!

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: [aside] O my husband – prevented – and what's almost as bad, found with my arms about another man – that will appear too much – what shall I say? – Sir Jasper come hither. I am trying if Mr Horner were ticklish, and he's as ticklish as can be. I love to torment the confounded toad; let you and I tickle him.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: No, your ladyship will tickle him better without me, I suppose. But is this your buying china? I thought you had been at the china house.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: [aside] China house, that's my cue, I must take it. – A pox! Can't you keep your impertinent wives at home? Some men are troubled with the husbands, but I with the wives. But I'd have you to know, since I cannot be your journeyman by night, I will not be your drudge by day, to squire your wife about and be your man of straw, or scarecrow, only to pies and jays that would be nibbling at your forbidden fruit. I shall be shortly the hackney gentleman-usher of the town.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: [aside] Heh, heh, he! Poor fellow, he's in the right on't, faith. To squire women about for other folks is as ungrateful an employment as to tell money for other folks. – Heh, he, he! Be't angry, Horner.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, 'tis I have more reason to be angry, who am left by you, to go abroad indecently alone; or, what is more indecent, to pin myself upon such ill-bred people of your acquaintance as this is.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Nay, prithee, what has he done?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Nay, he has done nothing.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: But what d'ye take ill, if he has done nothing?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Hah, hah, hah! Faith, I can't but laugh however. Why d'ye think the unmannerly toad would not come down to me to the coach? I was fain to come up to fetch him, or go without him, which I was resolved not to do; for he knows china very well, and has himself very good, but will not let me see it lest I should beg some. But I will find it out, and have what I came for yet.

div2.stage: Exit Lady Fidget, and locks the door, followed by Horner to the door.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: [apart to Lady Fidget] Lock the door, madam. (Aloud) So, she has got into my chamber, and locked me out. Oh, the impertinency of woman-kind! Well, Sir Jasper, plain dealing is a jewel; if ever you suffer your wife to trouble me again here, she shall carry you home a pair of horns, by my Lord Mayor she shall; though I cannot furnish you myself, you are sure, yet I'll find a way.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: [aside] Hah, ha, he! At my first coming in, and finding her arms about him, tickling him it seems, I was half jealous, but now I see my folly. – Heh, he, he! Poor Horner.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, though you laugh now, 'twill be my turn ere long. Oh women, more impertinent, more cunning, and more mischievous than their monkeys, and to me almost as ugly! Now is she throwing my things about, and rifling all I have, but I'll get into her the back way, and so rifle her for it –

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Hah, ha, ha! Poor angry Horner.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Stay here a little, I'll ferret her out to you presently, I warrant.

div2.stage: [Sir Jasper calls through the door to his wife, she answers from within]

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Wife! My Lady Fidget! Wife! He is coming into you the back way.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Let him come, and welcome, which way he will.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: He'll catch you, and use you roughly, and be too strong for you.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Don't you trouble yourself, let him if he can.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: [behind] This indeed, I could not have believed from him, nor any but my own eyes.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Where's this woman-hater, this toad, this ugly, greasy, dirty sloven?

p.seg: So, the women all will have him ugly. Methinks he is a comely person, but his wants make his form contemptible to 'em. And 'tis e'en as my wife said yesterday, talking of him, that a proper handsome eunuch was as ridiculous a thing as a gigantic coward.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Sir Jasper, your servant. Where is the odious beast?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: He's within in his chamber, with my wife. She's playing the wag with him.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Is she so? And he's a clownish beast, he'll give her no quarter, he'll play the wag with her again, let me tell you. Come, let's go help her. – What, the door's locked?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, my wife locked it –

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Did she so? Let us break it open then.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: No, no, he'll do her no hurt.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: No. – [Aside] But is there no other way to get into 'em? Whither goes this? I will disturb 'em.

div2.stage: Exit Mrs Squeamish at another door.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Where is this harlotry, this impudent baggage, this rambling tomrigg? O Sir Jasper, I'm glad to see you here. Did you not see my vild grandchild come in hither just now?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Ay, but where is she then? Where is she? Lord, Sir Jasper, I have e'en rattled myself to pieces in pursuit of her. But can you tell what she makes here? They say below, no woman lodges here.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: No! What does she here then? Say, if it be not a woman's lodging, what makes she here? But are you sure no woman lodges here?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: No, nor no man neither. This is Mr Horner's lodging.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Is it so? Are you sure?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: So; then there's no hurt in't, I hope. But where is he?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: He's in the next room with my wife.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Nay, if you trust him with your wife, I may with my Biddy. They say he's a merry harmless man now, e'en as harmless a man as ever came out of Italy with a good voice, and as pretty harmless company for a lady, as a snake without his teeth.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, ay, poor man.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: I can't find 'em. – Oh, are you here grandmother? I followed, you must know, My Lady Fidget hither; 'tis the prettiest lodging, and I have been staring on the prettiest pictures.

div2.stage: Enter Lady Fidget with a piece of china in her hand, and Horner following.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: And I have been toiling and moiling for the prettiest piece of china, my dear.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, she has been too hard for me, do what I could.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: O Lord, I'll have some china too, good Mr Horner. Don't think to give other people china, and me none. Come in with me too.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Upon my honour, I have none left now.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Nay, nay, I have known you deny your china before now, but you shan't put me off so. Come –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: This lady had the last there.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Yes indeed, madam, to my certain knowledge he has no more left.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Oh, but it may be he may have some you could not find.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: What? D'ye think if he had had any left, I would not have had it too? For we women of quality never think we have china enough.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Do not take it ill, I cannot make china for you all, but I will have a roll-wagon for you too another time.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Thank you, dear toad.

p.seg: What do you mean by that promise?
Alas, she has an innocent, literal understanding.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Poor Mr Horner, he has enough to do to please you all, I see.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, madam, you see how they use me.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Poor gentleman, I pity you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I thank you madam, I could never find pity, but from such reverend ladies as you are; the young ones will never spare a man.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Come come, beast, and go dine with us, for we shall want a man at hombre after dinner.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: That's all their use of me madam, you see.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Come sloven, I'll lead you to be sure of you.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Alas, poor man, how she tugs him! Kiss, kiss her, that's the way to make such nice women quiet.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No madam, that remedy is worse than the torment. They know I dare suffer anything rather than do it.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Prithee kiss her, and I'll give you her picture in little that you admired so last night; prithee do.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, nothing but that could bribe me; I love a woman only in effigy, and good painting as much as I hate them. I'll do't, for I could adore the devil well painted.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Foh, you filthy toad! Nay, now I've done jesting.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! I told you so.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Foh! A kiss of his –

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Has no more hurt in't than one of my spaniel's.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Nor no more good neither.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: [behind] I will now believe anything he tells me.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: O Lord, here's a man! Sir Jasper, my mask, my mask! I would not be seen here for the world.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: What, not when I am with you?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, no, my honour – let's be gone.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Oh, grandmother, let us be gone, make haste, make haste, I know not how he may censure us.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Be found in the lodging of anything like a man! Away!

div2.stage: Exeunt Sir Jasper, Lady Fidget, Old Lady Squeamish, Mrs Squeamish.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: [behind] What's here? Another cuckold? He looks like one, and none else, sure, have any business with him.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, what brings my dear friend hither?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Your impertinency –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: My impertinency? Why, you gentleman that have got handsome wives think you have a privilege of saying anything to your friends, and are as brutish as if you were our creditors.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No sir, I'll ne'er trust you any way.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But why not dear Jack? Why diffide in me thou know'st so well?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Because I do know you so well.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Han't I been always thy friend, honest Jack? Always ready to serve thee, in love, or battle, before thou wert married, and am so still?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I believe so; you would be my second now, indeed.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well then, dear Jack, why so unkind, so grum, so strange to me? Come, prithee kiss me, dear rogue. Gad, I was always I say, and am still as much thy servant as –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: As I am yours, sir. What, you would send a kiss to my wife, is that it?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So, there 'tis – a man can't shew his friendship to a married man, but presently he talks of his wife to you. Prithee, let thy wife alone, and let thee and I be all one, as we were wont. What, thou art as shy of my kindness as a Lumbard Street alderman of a courtier's civility at Locket's.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But you are overkind to me, as kind as if I were your cuckold already. Yet I must confess you ought to be kind and civil to me, since I am so kind, so civil to you as to bring you this. Look you there, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What is't?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Only a love letter sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: From whom? – how! This is from your wife! – hum – and – hum –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Even from my wife sir. Am I not wondrous kind and civil to you now too? – [Aside] But you'll not think her so.

p.seg: Ha! Is this a trick of his or hers?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: The gentleman's surprised I find. What, you expected a kinder letter?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No faith, not I, how could I?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes yes, I'm sure you did. A man so well made as you are must needs be disappointed if the woman declare not their passion at first sight or opportunity.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p:
But what should this mean? Stay, the postscript.
[Reads aside] 'Be sure you love me whatsoever my husband says to the contrary, and let him not see this, lest he should come home and pinch me, or kill my squirrel.'
[Aside] It seems he knows not what the letter contains.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, ne'er wonder at it so much.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Faith, I can't help it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Now I think I have deserved your infinite friendship and kindness, and have shewed myself sufficiently an obliging kind friend and husband. Am I not so, to bring a letter from my wife to her gallant?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, the devil take me, art thou, the most obliging, kind friend and husband in the world. Ha, ha!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, you may be merry sir, but in short I must tell you, sir, my honour will suffer no jesting.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What dost thou mean?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Does the letter want a comment? The know sir, though I have been so civil a husband as to bring you a letter from my wife, to let you kiss and court her to my face, I will not be a cuckold sir, I will not.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Thou art mad with jealousy. I never saw thy wife in my life but at the play yesterday, and I know not if it were she or no. I court her, kiss her!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I will not be a cuckold, I say. There will be danger in making me a cuckold.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, wert thou not well cured of thy last clap?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I wear a sword.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: It should be taken from thee, lest thou shouldst do thyself a mischief with it. Thou art mad, man.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: As mad as I am, and as merry as you are, I must have more reason from you ere we part. I say again, though you kissed and courted last night my wife in man's clothes, as she confesses in her letter –

p.seg: Ha!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Both she and I say you must not design it again, for you have mistaken your woman, as you have done your man.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: [Aside] Oh – I understand something now. – Was that thy wife? Why wouldst thou not tell me 'twas she? Faith, my freedom with her was your fault, not mine.

p.seg: Faith, so 'twas.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Fie! I'd never do't to a woman before her husband's face, sure.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But I had rather you should do't to my wife before my face than behind my back, and that you shall never do.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No – you will hinder me.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: If I would not hinder you, you see by her letter she would.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, I must e'en acquiesce then, and be contented with what she writes.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I'll assure you 'twas voluntarily writ. I had no hand in't, you may believe me.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I do believe thee, faith.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: And believe her too, for she's an innocent creature, has no dissembling in her. And so fare you well, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Pray, however, present my humble service to her, and tell her I will obey her letter to a tittle, and fulfil her desires be what they will, or with what difficulty soever I do't, and you shall be no more jealous of me, I warrant her, and you.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well then, fare you well, and play with any man's honour but mine, kiss any man's wife but mine, and welcome.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! Doctor.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: [coming out] It seems he has not heard the report of you, or does not believe it.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ha, ha! Now, doctor, what think you?

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Pray let's see the letter [reads the letter] – hum – 'for – dear – love you' –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I wonder how she could contrive it? What say'st thou to't? 'Tis an original.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: So are your cuckolds too, originals, for they are like no other common cuckolds; and I will henceforth believe it not impossible for you to cuckold the Grand Signior amidst his guards of eunuchs, that I say.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And I say for the letter, 'tis the first love letter that ever was without flames, darts, fates, destinies, lying and dissembling in't.

div2.stage: Enter Sparkish pulling in Mr Pinchwife.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come back, you are a pretty brother-in-law, neither go to church, nor to dinner with your sister bride!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: My sister denies her marriage, and you see is gone away from you dissatisfied.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw! Upon a foolish scruple that our parson was not in lawful orders, and did not say all the Common Prayer; but 'tis her modesty only, I believe. But let women be never so modest the first day, they'll be sure to come to themselves by night, and I shall have enough of her then. In the meantime, Harry Horner, you must dine with me. I keep my wedding at my aunt's in the Piazza.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Thy wedding! What stale maid has lived to despair of a husband, or what young one of a gallant?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Oh, your servant, sir – this gentleman's sister then – no stale maid.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I'm sorry for't.

p.seg: How comes he so concerned for her?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: You sorry for't? Why, do you know any ill by her?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, I know none but by thee. 'Tis for her sake, not yours, and another man's sake that might have hoped, I thought.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Another man, another man? What is his name?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, since 'tis past he shall be nameless. – [Aside] Poor Harcourt, I am sorry thou hast missed her.

p.seg: He seems to be much troubled at the match –

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Prithee tell me – nay, you shan't go, brother.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I must of necessity, but I'll come to you to dinner.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: But Harry, what, have I a rival in my wife already? But with all my heart, for he may be of use to me hereafter. For though my hunger is now my sauce, and I can fall on heartily without, but the time will come when a rival will be as good sauce for a married man to a wife as an orange to veal.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: O thou damned rogue! Thou hast set my teeth on edge with thy orange.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Then let's to dinner – there, I was with you again. Come.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But who dines with thee?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: My friends and relations. My brother Pinchwife you see, of your acquaintance.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And his wife?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No gad, he'll ne'er let her come amongst us good fellows. Your stingy country coxcomb keeps his wife from his friends as he does his little firkin of ale for his own drinking, and a gentleman can't get a smack on't; but his servants, when his back is turned, broach it at their pleasures, and dust it away. Ha, ha, ha! Gad, I am witty, I think, considering I was married today, by the world. But come –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, I will not dine with you, unless you can fetch her too.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Pshaw! What pleasure canst thou have with women now, Harry?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: My eyes are not gone; I love a good prospect yet, and will not dine with you unless she does too. Go fetch her therefore, but do not tell her husband 'tis for my sake.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Well, I'll go try what I can do. In the meantime come away, to my aunt's lodging, 'tis in the way to Pinchwife's.

p.seg: The poor woman has called for aid, and stretched forth her hand, doctor; I cannot but help her over the pale out of the briars.

div2.head: SCENE FOUR
div2.stage: The scene changes to Pinchwife's house.
Mrs Pinchwife alone, leaning on her elbow. A table, pen, ink and paper.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, 'tis e'en so; I have got the London disease they call love. I am sick of my husband, and for my gallant. I have heard this distemper called a fever but methinks 'tis liker an ague, for when I think of my husband I tremble and am in a cold sweat and have inclinations to vomit; but when I think of my gallant, dear Mr Horner, my hot fit comes and I am all in a fever, indeed, and as in other fevers my own chamber is tedious to me, and I would fain be removed to his, and then methinks I should be well. Ah, poor Mr Horner! Well, I cannot, will not stay here, therefore I'll make an end of my letter to him, which shall be a finer letter than my last, because I have studied it like anything; O sick, sick!

div2.stage: Enter Mr Pinchwife who seeing her writing steals softly behind her, and looking over her shoulder, snatches the paper from her.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, writing more letters?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O lord bud, why d'ye fright me so?

div2.stage: [She offers to run out: he stops her and reads.]

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
How's this? Nay, you shall not stir, madam. 'Dear, dear, dear, Mr Horner' – very well – I have taught you to write letters to good purpose – but let's see't. 'First, I am to beg your pardon for my boldness in writing to you, which I'd have you to know I would not have done, had not you said first you loved me so extremely, which if you do, you will never suffer me to lie in the arms of another man, whom I loathe, nauseate, and detest.' – Now you can write these filthy words. But what follows? – 'Therefore I hope you will speedily find some way to free me from this unfortunate match, which was never, I assure you, of my choice, but I'm afraid 'tis already too far gone. However, if you love me, as I do you, you will try what you can do, but you must help me away before tomorrow, or else, alas I shall be for ever out of your reach, for I can defer no longer our' – 'our' –
[the letter concludes] what is to follow 'our'? – Speak, what? Our journey into the country, I suppose? – Oh woman, damned woman, and love, damned love, their old tempter! For this is one of his miracles; in a moment he can make those blind that could see, and those see that were blind, those dumb that could speak, and those prattle who were dumb before. Nay, what is more than all, make these dow-baked, senseless, indocile animals, women, too hard for us, their politic lords and rulers, in a moment. But make an end of your letter, and then I'll make an end of you thus, and all my plagues together.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O Lord, O Lord, you are such a passionate man, bud!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: How now, what's here to do?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: This fool here now!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: What, drawn upon your wife? You should never do that but at night in the dark when you can't hurt her. This is my sister-in-law is it not? [Pulls aside her handkerchief.] Ay, faith, e'en our country Margery, one may know her. Come, she and you must go dine with me; dinner's ready, come. But where's my wife? Is she not come home yet? Where is she?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Making you a cuckold; 'tis that they all do, as soon as they can.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: What, the wedding day? No, a wife that designs to make a cully of her husband will be sure to let him win the first stake of love, by the world. But come, they stay dinner for us. Come, I'll lead down our Margery.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No – sir, go, we'll follow you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: I will not wag without you.

p.seg: This coxcomb is a sensible torment to me amidst the greatest in the world.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, come, Madam Margery.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
No, I'll lead her my way. What, would you treat your friends with mine, for want of your own wife? [Leads her to t'other door, and locks her in and returns.]
[Aside] I am contented my rage should take breath.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: I told Horner this.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come now.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Lord how shy you are of your wife! But let me tell you, brother, we men of wit have amongst us a saying that cuckolding, like the smallpox, comes with a fear; and you may keep your wife as much as you will out of danger of infection, but if her constitution incline her to't, she'll have it sooner or later, by the world, say they.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] What a thing is a cuckold, that every fool can make him ridiculous! – Well sir – but let me advise you, now you are come to be concerned, because you suspect the danger, not to neglect the means to prevent it, especially when the greatest share of the malady will light upon your own head, for –

lg.l: How s'e'er the kind wife's belly comes to swell.
The husband breeds for her, and first is ill.

div2.head: SCENE ONE
div2.stage: Enter Mr Pinchwife and Mrs Pinchwife. A table and candle.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, take the pen and make an end of the letter, just as you intended. If you are false in a tittle, I shall soon perceive it, and punish you with this as you deserve.

div2.stage: [Lays his hand on his sword.] PR}Write what was to follow – let's see – 'You must take haste and help me away before tomorrow, or else I shall be for ever out of your reach, for I can defer no longer our' – What follows 'our'? –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
Must all out then, bud?
[Mrs Pinchwife takes the pen and writes.] Look you there then.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let's see – 'For I can defer no longer our – wedding – Your slighted Alithea.' What's the meaning of this? My sister's name to't? Speak, unriddle!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes indeed, bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But why her name to't? Speak – speak, I say!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Ay, but you'll tell her then again; if you would not tell her again –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I will not – I am stunned, my head turns round. Speak!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Won't you tell her indeed, and indeed?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No. Speak, I say!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: She'll be angry with me, but I had rather she should be angry with me than you, bud; and to tell you the truth, 'twas she made me write the letter, and taught me what I should write.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: (aside) Ha! I thought the style was somewhat better than her own. – But how could she come to you to teach you, since I had locked you up alone?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O – through the keyhold, bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But why should she make you write a letter for her to him, since she can write herself?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, she said because – for I was unwilling to do it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Because what – because?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Because, lest Mr Horner should be cruel, and refuse her, or vain afterwards, and shew the letter, she might disown it, the hand not being hers.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] How's this? Ha! Then I think I shall come to myself again. This changeling could not invent this lie, but if she could, why should she? She might think I should soon discover it – stay – now I think on't too, Horner said he was sorry she had married Sparkish, and her disowning her marriage to me makes me think she has evaded it for Horner's sake. Yet why should she take this course? But men in love are fools, women may well be so. – But hark you madam, your sister went out in the morning, and I have not seen her within since.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Alackaday, she has been crying all day above, it seems, in a corner.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Where is she? Let me speak with her.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] O Lord, then he'll discover all. – Pray hold, bud; what, d'ye mean to discover me? She'll know I have told you then. Pray bud, let me talk with her first.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I must speak with her to know whether Horner ever made her any promise, and whether she be married to Sparkish or no.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray dear bud don't, till I have spoken with her and told her that I have told you all, for she'll kill me else.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Go then, and bid her come out to me.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Yes, yes, bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let me see –

p.seg: I'll go, but she is not within to come to him. I have just got time to know of Lucy her maid, who first set me on work, what lie I shall tell next, for I am e'en at my wits end.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Well, I resolve it; Horner shall have her. I'd rather give him my sister than lend him my wife, and such an alliance will prevent his pretensions to my wife, sure. I'll make him of kin to her, and then he won't care for her.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O Lord, bud, I told you what anger you would make me with my sister.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Won't she come hither?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, no, alackaday, she's ashamed to look you in the face, and she says if you go in to her, she'll run away downstairs, and shamefully go herself to Mr Horner, who has promised her marriage, she says, and she will have no other, so she won't.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
Did he so – promise her marriage? – Then she shall have no other. Go tell her so, and if she will come and discourse with me a little concerning the means, I will about it immediately. Go. Exit MRS PINCHWIFE.
His estate is equal to Sparkish's, and his extraction as much better than his as his parts are; but my chief reason is, I'd rather be of kin to him by the name of brother-in-law than that of cuckold. Enter MRS PINCHWIFE.
Well, what says she now?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, she says she would only have you lead her to Horner's lodging – with whom she first will discourse the matter before she talk with you, which yet she cannot do; for alack, poor creature, she says she can't so much as look you in the face. Therefore she'll come to you in a mask, and you must excuse her if she make you no answer to any question of yours, till you have brought her to Mr Horner; and if you will not chide her, nor question her, she'll come out to you immediately.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Let her come; I will not speak a word to her, nor require a word from her.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, I forgot; besides, she says she cannot look you in the face though through a mask, therefore would desire you to put out the candle.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p:
I agree to all; let her make haste. There, 'tis out. [Put out the candle.] My case is something better, I'd rather fight with Horner for not lying with my sister than for lying with my wife, and of the two I had rather find my sister too forward than my wife. I expected no other from her free education, as she calls it, and her passion for the town. Well – wife and sister are names which make us expect love and duty, pleasure and comfort, but we find 'em plagues and torments, and are equally, though differently, troublesome to their keeper; for we have as much ado to get people to lie with our sisters as to keep 'em from lying with our wives. Enter Mrs Pinchwife masked, and in hoods and scarves, and a nightgown and petticoat of Alithea's, in the dark.
What, are you come sister? Let us go then – but first let me lock up my wife. Mrs Margery, where are you?

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Here, bud.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come hither, that I may lock you up. [Locks the door.] Get you in. Come sister, where are you now?

div2.stage: Mrs Pinchwife gives him her hand, but when he lets her go, she steals softly on t'other side of him, and is led away by him for his sister Alithea.

div2.head: SCENE TWO
div2.stage: The scene changes to Horner's lodging.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: What, all alone? Not so much as one of your cuckolds here, nor one of their wives! They use to take their turns with you, as if they were to watch you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
