sp.p: Yes, it often happens that a cuckold is but his wife's spy, and is more upon family duty when he is with her gallant abroad hindering his pleasure than when he is at home with her playing the gallant. But the hardest duty a married women imposes upon a lover is keeping her husband company always.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: And his fondness wearies you almost as soon as hers.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: A pox! Keeping a cuckold company after you have had his wife is as tiresome as the company of a country squire to a witty fellow of the town when he has got all his money.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: And as at first a man makes a friend of the husband to get the wife, so at last you are fain to fall out with the wife to be rid of the husband.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, most cuckold-makers are true courtiers; when once a poor man has cracked his credit for 'em, they can't abide to come near him.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: But at first, to draw him in, are so sweet, so kind, so dear, just as you are to Pinchwife. But what becomes of that intrigue with his wife?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: A pox! He's as surly as an alderman that has been bit, and since he's so coy, his wife's kindness is in vain, for she's a silly innocent.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Did she not send you a letter by him?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Yes, but that's a riddle I have not yet solved. Allow the poor creature to be willing, she is silly too, and he keeps her up so close –

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Yes, so close that he makes her but the more willing, and adds but revenge to her love, which two when met seldom fail of satisfying each other one way or other.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What! Here's the man we are talking of, I think.

div2.stage: Enter Mr Pinchwife, leading in his wife masked, muffled, and in her sister's gown.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Pshaw!

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Bringing his wife to you is the next thing to bringing a love letter from her.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What means this?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: The last time, you know, sir, I brought you a love letter; now, you see, a mistress. I think you'll say I am a civil man to you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, the devil take me, will I say thou art the civillest man I ever met with, and I have known some. I fancy I understand thee now better than I did the letter; but hark thee, in thy ear –

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nothing but the usual question man: is she sound, on thy word?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, you take her for a wench, and me for a pimp?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Pshaw! Wench and pimp, paw words. I know thou art an honest fellow, and hast a great acquaintance among the ladies, and perhaps hast made love for me rather than let me make love to thy wife.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come sir, in short, I am for no fooling.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nor I either. Therefore, prithee, let's see her face presently. Make her show, man; art thou sure I don't know her?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I am sure you do know her.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: A pox! Why dost thou bring her to me then?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Because she's a relation of mine –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Is she, faith, man? Then thou art still more civil and obliging, dear rogue.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: – who desired me to bring her to you.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Then she is obliging, dear rogue.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: You'll make her welcome for my sake, I hope.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I hope she is handsome enough to make herself welcome. Prithee let her unmask.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Do you speak to her; she would never be ruled by me.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p:
Madam –
[Mrs Pinchwife whispers to Horner.] She says she must speak with me in private. Withdraw, prithee.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside] She's unwilling, it seems, I should know all her undecent conduct in this business. – Well then, I'll leave you together, and hope when I am gone you'll agree; if not, you and I shan't agree, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: What means the fool? If she and I agree 'tis no matter what you and I do.

div2.stage: [Whispers to Mrs Pinchwife, who makes signs with her hand for him (Pinchwife) to be gone.]

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: In the meantime I'll fetch a parson, and find out Sparkish and disabuse him. – You would have me fetch a parson, would you not? Well then – now I think I am rid of her, and shall have no more trouble with her. Our sisters and daughters, like usurers' money, are safest when put out; but our wives, like their writings, never safe but in our closets under lock and key.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Sir Jasper Fidget, sir, is coming up.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Here's the trouble of a cuckold, now we are talking of. A pox on him! Has he not enough to do to hinder his wife's sport, but he must other women's too? – Step in here, madam.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: My best and dearest friend.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: (aside to Quack) The old style, doctor. – Well, be short, for I am busy. What would your impertinent wife have now?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Well guessed, i'faith, for I do come from her.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: To invite me to supper? Tell her I can't come; go.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Nay, now you are out, faith; for my lady and the whole knot of the virtuous gang, as they call themselves, are resolved upon a frolic of coming to you tonight in a masquerade, and are all dressed already.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I shan't be at home.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Lord, how churlish he is to women! – Nay, prithee don't disappoint 'em. They'll think 'tis my fault; prithee don't. I'll send in the banquet and the fiddles, but make no noise on't, for the poor virtuous rogues would not have it known for the world that they go a-masquerading, and they would come to no man's ball but yours.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well, well. – Get you gone, and tell 'em if they come, 'twill be at the peril of their honour and yours.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Heh, he, he! – we'll trust you for that. Farewell.

lg.l: Doctor, anon you too shall be my guest,
But now I'm going to a private feast.

div2.head: SCENE THREE
div2.stage: The scene changes to the piazza of Covent Garden.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: [with the letter in his hands] But who would have thought a woman could have been false to me? By the world, I could not have thought it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: You were for giving and taking liberty; she has taken it only, sir, now you find in that letter. You are a frank person, and so is she, you see there.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, if this be her hand – for I never saw it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Tis no matter whether that be her hand or no, I am sure this hand at her desire led her to Mr Horner, with whom I left her just now, to go fetch a parson to 'em at their desire too, to deprive you of her for ever, for it seems yours was but a mock marriage.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Indeed, she would needs have it that 'twas Harcourt himself in a parson's habit that married us, but I'm sure he told me 'twas his brother Ned.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, there 'tis out and you were deceived, not she, for you are such a frank person – but I must be gone. You'll find her at Mr Horner's; go and believe your eyes.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p:
Nay, I'll to her, and call her as many crocodiles, sirens, harpies, and other heathenish names as a poet would do a mistress who had refused to hear his suit, nay more, his verses on her. – But stay, is not that she following a torch at t'other end of the Piazza? And from Horner's certainly – 'tis so. Enter Alithea following a torch, and Lucy behind.
You are well met, madam, though you don't think so. What, you have made a short visit to Mr Horner? But I suppose you'll return to him presently; but that time the parson can be with him.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Mr Horner and the parson, sir?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Come, madam, no more dissembling, no more jilting, for I am no more a frank person.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: How's this?

p.seg: So, 'twill work, I see.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Could you find out no easy country fool to abuse? None but me, a gentleman of wit and pleasure about the town? But it was your pride to be too hard for a man of parts, unworthy false woman! False as a friend that lends a man money to lose, false as dice, who undo those that trust all day have to 'em.

p.seg: He has been a great bubble by his similes, as they say.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: You have been too merry, sir, at your wedding dinner, sure.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: What, d'ye mock me too?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Or you have been deluded.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: By you.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Let me understand you.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Have you the confidence – I should call it something else, since you know your guilt – to stand my just reproaches? You did not write an impudent letter to Mr Horner, who I find now has clubbed with you in deluding me with his aversion for women, that I might not, forsooth, suspect him for my rival?

p.seg: D'ye think the gentleman can be jealous now, madam?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: I write a letter to Mr Horner!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Nay, madam, do not deny it. Your brother shewed it me just now, and told me likewise he left you at Horner's lodging to fetch a parson to marry you to him. And I wish you joy madam, joy, joy, and to him too, much joy, and to myself more joy for not marrying you.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: [aside] So, I find my brother would break off the match, and I can consent t'ot, since I see this gentleman can be made jealous. – O Lucy, by his rude usage and jealousy he makes me almost afraid I am married to him. Art thou sure 'twas Harcourt himself and no parson that married us?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: No, madam, I thank you. I suppose that was a contrivance too of Mr Horner's and yours, to make Harcourt play the parson. But I would as little as you have him one now, no, not for the world. For shall I tell you another truth? I never had any passion for you till now, for now I hate you. 'Tis true I might have married your portion, as other men of parts of the town do sometimes; and so your servant. And to shew my unconcernedness, I'll come to your wedding, and resign you with as much joy as I would a stale wench to a new cully, nay with as much joy as I would after the first night, if I had been married to you. There's for you, and so your servant, servant.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: How was I deceived in a man!

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: You'll believe then a fool may be made jealous now? For that easiness in him that suffers him to be led by a wife will likewise permit him to be persuaded against her by others.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: But marry Mr Horner! My brother does not intend it, sure; if I thought he did, I would take thy advice, and Mr Harcourt for my husband. And now I wish that if there be any over-wise woman of the town, who, like me, would marry a fool for fortune, liberty, or title, first that her husband may love play, and be a cully to all the town but her, and suffer none but fortune to be mistress of his purse. Then, if for liberty, that he may send her into the country under the conduct of some housewifely mother-in-law. And if for title, may the world give 'em none but that of cuckold.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: And for her greater curse, madam, may he not deserve it.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Away, impertinent! – Is not this my old Lady Lanterlu's?

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Yes, madam. – [Aside] And here I hope we shall find Mr Harcourt.

div2.head: SCENE FOUR
div2.stage: The scene changes again to Horner's lodging.
Horner, Lady Fidget, Mrs Dainty Fidget, Mrs Squeamish. A table, banquet, and bottles.

p.seg: A pox! They are come too soon – before I have sent back my new mistress. All I have now to do is to lock her in, that they may not see her.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: That we may be sure of our welcome, we have brought our entertainment with us, and are resolved to treat thee, dear toad.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: And that we may be merry to purpose, have left Sir Jasper and my old Lady Squeamish quarrelling at home at baggammon.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Therefore let us make use of our time lest they should chance to interrupt us.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Let us sit then.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: First, that you may be private, let me lock this door, and that, and I'll wait upon you presently.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No sir, shut 'em only and your lips for ever, for we must trust you as much as our women.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: You know all vanity's killed in me, I have no occasion for talking.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Now, ladies, supposing we had drank each of us our two bottles, let us speak the truth of our hearts.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET and MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Agreed.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: By this brimmer, for truth is nowhere else to be found. [Aside to Horner] Not in thy heart, false man.

p.seg: You have found me a true man, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: [aside to Horner] Not every way. – But let us sit and be merry.

lg.l: Why should our damned tyrants oblige us to live
On the pittance of pleasure which they only give?
We must not rejoice,
With wine and with noise,
In vain we must wake in a dull bed alone,
Whilst to our warm rival, the bottle, they're gone.
Then lay aside charms,
And take up these arms.*
'Tis wine only gives 'em their courage and wit;
Because we live sober, to men we submit.
If for beauties you'd pass,
Take a lick of the glass,
'Twill mend your complexions, and when they are gone,
The best red we have is the red of the grape.
Then sisters, lay't on.
And damn a good shape.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Dear brimmer! Well, in token of our openness and plain dealing, let us throw our masks over our heads.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: So, 'twill come to the glasses anon.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Lovely brimmer! Let me enjoy him first.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, I never part with a gallant till I've tried him. Dear brimmer, that makest our husbands short-sighted.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: And our bashful gallants bold.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And for want of a gallant, the butler lovely in our eyes. – Drink, eunuch.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Drink, thou representative of a husband. Damn a husband!

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: And, as it were a husband, an old keeper.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And an old grandmother.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And an English bawd, and a French chirurgeon.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Ay, we have all reason to curse 'em.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: For my sake, ladies?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, for our own, for the first spoils all young gallants' industry.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: And the other's art makes 'em bold only with common women.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And rather run the hazard of the vile distemper amongst them than of a denial amongst us.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: The filthy toads choose mistresses now as they do stuffs, for having been fancied and worn by others.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: For being common and cheap.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Whilst women of quality, like the richest stuffs, lie untumbled and unasked for.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ay, neat, and cheap, and new, often they think best.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: No sir, the beasts will be known by a mistress longer than by a suit.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And 'tis not for cheapness neither.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, for the vain fops will take up druggets and embroider 'em. But I wonder at the depraved appetites of witty men; they use to be out of the common road, and hate imitation. Pray tell me, beast, when you were a man, why you rather chose to club with a multitude in a common house for an entertainment than to be the only guest at a good table.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, faith, ceremony and expectation are unsufferable to those that are sharp bent. People always eat with the best stomach at an ordinary, where every man is snatching for the best bit.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Though he get a cut over the fingers. But I have heard people eat most heartily of another man's meat, that is, what they do not pay for.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: When they are sure of their welcome and freedom, for ceremony in love and eating is as ridiculous as in fighting; falling on briskly is all should be done in those occasions.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Well, then, let me tell you, sir, there is nowhere more freedom than in our houses, and we take freedom from a young person as a sign of good breeding, and a person may be as free as he pleases with us, as frolic, as gamesome, as wild as he will.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Ha'n't I heard you all declaim against wild men?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Yes, but for all that, we think wildness in a man as desirable a quality as in a duck or rabbit; a tame man, foh!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I know not, but your reputations frightened me as much as your faces invited me.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Our reputation! Lord, why should you not think that we women make use of our reputation, as you men of yours, only to deceive the world with less suspicion? Our virtue is like the statesman's religion, the quaker's word, the gamester's oath, and the great man's honour, but to cheat those that trust us.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And that demureness, coyness, and modesty that you see in our faces in the boxes at plays is as much a sign of a kind woman as a vizard-mask in the pit.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: For, I assure you, women are least masked when they have the velvet vizard on.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: You would have found us modest women in our denials only.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Our bashfulness is only the reflection of the men's.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: We blush when they are shame-faced.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I beg your pardon, ladies, I was deceived in you devilishly. But why that mighty pretence to honour?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: We have told you. But sometimes 'twas for the same reason you men pretend business often, to avoid ill company, to enjoy the better and more privately those you love.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: But why would you ne'er give a friend a wink then?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Faith, you reputation frightened us as much as ours did you. You were so notoriously lewd.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And you so seemingly honest.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Was that all that deterred you?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And so expensive – you allow freedom you say –

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Ay, ay.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: That I was afraid of losing my little money, as well as my little time, both which my other pleasures required.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Money, foh! You talk like a little fellow now. Do such as we expect money?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I beg your pardon, madam, I must confess I have heard that great ladies, like great merchants, set but the higher prices upon what they have, because they are not in necessity of taking the first offer.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Such as we make sale of our hearts?

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: We bribed for our love? Foh!

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: With your pardon, ladies, I know, like great men in offices, you seem to exact flattery and attendance only from your followers; but you have receivers about you, and such fees to pay, a man is afraid to pass your grants. Besides, we must let you win at cards, or we lose your hearts; and if you make an assignation, 'tis at a goldsmith's, jeweller's, or china house, where, for your honour you deposit to him, he must pawn his to the punctual cit, and so paying for what you take up, pays for what he takes up.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: Would you not have us assured of our gallants' love?

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: For love is better known by liberality than by jelousy.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: For one may be dissembled, the other not. – [Aside] But my jealousy can be no longer dissembled, and they are telling-ripe. – Come, here's to our gallants in waiting, whom we must name, and I'll begin. This is my false rogue.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: How!

p.seg: So all will out now.
Did you not tell me 'twas for my sake only you reported yourself no man?
O wretch! Did you not swear to me 'twas for my love and honour you passed for that thing you do?
So, so.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Come, speak, ladies; this is my false villain.

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And mine too.

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: And mine.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Well then, you are all three my false rogues too, and there's an end on't.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Well then, there's no remedy. Sister sharers, let us not fall out, but have a care of our honour. Though we get no presents, no jewels of him, we are savers of our honour, the jewel of most value and use, which shines yet to the world unsuspected, though it be counterfeit.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Nay, and is e'en as good as if it were true, provided the world think so; for honour, like beauty now, only depends on the opinion of others.

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: Well, Harry Common, I hope you can be true to three. Swear – but 'tis no purpose to require your oath, for you are as often forsworn as you swear to new women.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Come, faith, madam, let us e'en pardon one another, for all the difference I find betwixt we men and you women, we forswear ourselves at the beginning of an amour, you as long as it lasts.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Jarper Fidget and Old Lady Squeamish.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Oh, my Lady Fidget, was this your cunning, to come to Mr Horner without me? But you have been nowhere else, I hope?

sp.speaker: LADY FIDGET
sp.p: No, Sir Jasper.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: And you came straight hither, Biddy?

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Yes indeed, Lady Grandmother.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: 'Tis well. 'tis well. I knew when once they were throughly acquainted with poor Horner, they'd ne'er be from him. You may let her masquerade it with my wife and Horner, and I warrant her reputation safe.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: O sir, here's the gentleman come whom you bid me not suffer to come up without giving you notice, with a lady too, and other gentleman.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Do you all go in there, whilst I send 'em away, and boy, do you desire 'em to stay below till I come, which shall be immediately.

div2.stage: Exeunt Sir Jasper, Lady Squeamish, Lady Fidget, Mrs Dainty Fidget, Mrs Squeamish.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Yes sir.

div2.stage: Exit Horner at t'other door, and returns with Mrs Pinchwife.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: You would not take my advice to be gone home before your husband came back; he'll now discover all. Yet pray, my dearest, be persuaded to go home and leave to rest to my management. I'll let you down the back way.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I don't know the way home, so I don't.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: My man shall wait upon you.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: No, don't you believe that I'll go at all. What, are you weary of me already?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, my life, 'tis that I may love you long. 'Tis to secure my love, and your reputation with your husband. He'll never receive you again else.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What care I? D'ye think to frighten me with that? I don't intend to go to him again. You shall be my husband now.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: I cannot be your husband, dearest, since you are married to him.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oh, would you make me believe that? Don't I see, every day at London here, women leave their first husbands and go and live with other men as their wives? Pish, pshaw! You'd make me angry, but that I love you so mainly.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p:
So, they are coming up. – In again, in, I hear 'em: [Exit Mrs Pinchwife].
Well, a silly mistress is like a weak place, soon got, soon lost; a man has scarce time for plunder. She betrays her husband first to her gallant, and then her gallant to her husband.

div2.stage: Enter Pinchwife, Alithea, Harcourt, Sparkish, Lucy, and a parson.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, madam, 'tis not the sudden change of your dress, the confidence of your asseverations, and your false witness there, shall persuade me I did not bring you hither, just now. Here's my witness, who cannot deny it, since you must be confronted. – Mr Horner, did not I bring this lady to you just now?

p.seg: Now must I wrong one woman for another's sake, but that's no new thing with me; for in these cases I am still on the criminal's side, against the innocent.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Pray, speak, sir.

p.seg: It must be so – I must be impudent, and try my luck; impudence uses to be too hard for truth.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What, you are studying an evasion or excuse for her. Speak, sir.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, faith, I am something backward only to speak in women's affairs or disputes.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: She bids you speak.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Ay, pray sir, do. Pray satisfy him.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Then, truly, you did bring that lady to me just now.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Oho!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: How, sir!

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: How, Horner!

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: What mean you, sir? I always took you for a man of honour.

p.seg: Ay, so much a man of honour that I must save my mistress, I thank you, come what will on't.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: So, if I had had her, she'd have made me believe the moon had been made of a Christmas pie.

p.seg: Now could I speak, if I durst, and 'solve the riddle, who am the author of it.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: O unfortunate woman! (To Harcourt) A combination against my honour which most concerns me now because you share in my disgrace, sir, and it is your censure which I must now suffer that troubles me, not theirs.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Madam, then have no trouble, you shall now see 'tis possible for me to love too, without being jealous. I will not only believe your innocence myself, but make all the world believe it. – [Apart to Horner] Horner, I must now be concerned for this lady's honour.

p.seg: And I must be concerned for a lady's honour too.
This lady has her honour, and I will protect it.
My lady has not her honour, but has given it me to keep, and I will preserve it.
I understand you not.
I would not have you.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [peeping in behind] What's the matter with 'em all?

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Come, come, Mr Horner, no more disputing. Here's the parson, I brought him not in vain.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No sir, I'll employ him, if this lady please.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: How, what d'ye mean?

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ay, what does he mean?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Why, I have resigned your sister to him. He has my consent.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But he has no mine, sir. A woman's injured honour, no more than a man's, can be repaired or satisfied by any but him that first wronged it; and you shall marry her presently, or –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: O Lord, they'll kill poor Mr Horner! Besides, he shan't marry her whilst I stand by and look on. I'll not lose my second husband so.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: What do I see?

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: My sister in my clothes!

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [To Mr Pinchwife] Nay, pray now don't quarrel about finding work for the parson; he shall marry me to Mr Horner, for now, I believe, you have enough of me.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Damned, damned loving changeling!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Pray, sister, pardon me for telling so many lies of you.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I suppose the riddle is plain now.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: No, that must be my work. Good sir, hear me.

div2.stage: [Kneels to Mr Pinchwife, who stands doggedly, with his hat over his eyes.]

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I will never hear woman again, but make 'em all silent, thus –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: No, that must not be.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: You then shall go first, 'tis all one to me.

div2.stage: [Offers to draw on Horner; stopped by Harcourt.]

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: Hold!

div2.stage: Enter Sir Jasper Fidget, Lady Fidget, Lady Squeamish, Mrs Dainty Fidget, Mrs Squeamish.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: What's the matter, what's the matter? Pray what's the matter, sir? I beseech you, communicate, sir.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Why, my wife has communicated, sir, as your wife may have done too, sir, if she knows him, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Pshaw! With him? Ha, ha, he!

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: D'ye mock me, sir? A cuckold is a kind of a wild beast. Have a care, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: No sure, you mock me, sir – he cuckold you! It can't be, ha, ha, he! Why, I'll tell you, sir.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I tell you again, he has whored my wife, and yours too, if he knows her, and all the women he comes near. 'Tis not his dissembling, his hypocrisy, can wheedle me.

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: How! Does he dissemble? Is he a hypocrite? Nay then – how – wife – sister, is he an hypocrite?

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: An hypocrite! A dissembler! Speak, young harlotry, speak, how?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Nay then – Oh, my head too! – O thou libidinous lady!

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: O thou harloting harlotry! Hast thou done't then?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Speak, good Horner, art thou a dissembler, a rogue? Hast thou –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Soh!

p.seg: I'll fetch you off, and her too, if she will but hold her tongue.
Canst thou? I'll give thee –

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: (to Mr Pinchwife) Pray, have but patience to hear me, sir, who am the unfortunate cause of all this confusion. Your wife is innocent, I only culpable; for I put her upon telling you all these lies concerning my mistress, in order to the breaking off the match between Mr Sparkish and her, to make way for Mr Harcourt.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: Did you so, eternal rotten-tooth? Then it seems my mistress was not false to me, I was only deceived by you. Brother that should have been, now, man of conduct, who is a frank person now? To bring your wife to her lover – ha!

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: I assure you, sir, she came not to Mr Horner out of love, for she loves him no more –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Hold, I told lies for you, but you shall tell none for me, for I do love Mr Horner with all my soul, and nobody shall say me nay. Pray don't you go to make poor Mr Horner believe to the contrary, 'tis spitefully done of you, I'm sure.

p.seg: Peace, dear idiot!

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Nay, I will not peace.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: Not till I make you.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Horner, your servant. I am the doctor's guest, he must excuse our intrusion.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: But what's the matter, gentlemen? For heaven's sake, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Oh, 'tis well you are come. 'Tis a censorious world we live in. You may have brought me a reprieve, or else I had died for a crime I never committed, and these innocent ladies had suffered with me; therefore pray satisfy these worthy, honourable, jealous gentlemen – that -

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p:
Oh, I understand you; is that all? – Sir Jasper, by heavens and upon the word of a physician,
[whispers to Sir Jasper] sir, -

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Nay, I do believe you truly. – Pardon me, my virtuous lady, and dear of honour.

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: What, then all's right again?

sp.speaker: SIR JASPER
sp.p: Ay, ay, and now let us satisfy him too.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: An eunuch! Pray, no fooling with me.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: I'll bring half the chirurgeons in town to swear it.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: They! They'll swear a man that bled to death through his wounds died of an apoplexy.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Pray hear me, sir – why all the town has heard the report of him.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But does all the town believe it?

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: Pray inquire a little, and first, of all these.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: I'm sure when I left the town he was the lewdest fellow in't.

sp.speaker: QUACK
sp.p: I tell you, sir, he has been in France since. Pray ask but these ladies and gentlemen, your friend Mr Dorilant. Gentlemen and ladies, ha'n't you all heard the late sad repor of poor Mr Horner?

sp.speaker: ALL THE LADIES
sp.p: Ay, ay, ay.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: Why, thou jealous fool, dost thou doubt it? He's an arrant French capon.

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: 'Tis false, sir, you shall not disparage poor Mr Horner, for to my certain knowledge –

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Oh hold!

p.seg: Stop her mouth –

sp.speaker: OLD LADY SQUEAMISH
sp.p: [to Pinchwife] Upon my honour sir, 'tis as true –

sp.speaker: MRS DAINTY FIDGET
sp.p: D'ye think we would have been seen in his company?

sp.speaker: MRS SQUEAMISH
sp.p: Trust our unspotted reputations with him?

p.seg: This you get, and we too, by trusting your secret to a fool –

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Peace, madam. – [Aside to Quack] Well, doctor, is not this a good design that carries a man on unsuspected, and brings him off safe.

p.seg: Well, if this were true, but my wife –

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: Come, brother, your wife is yet innocent, you see. But have a care of too strong an imagination, lest like an over-concerned timorous gamester, by fancying an unlucky cast, it should come. Women and fortune are truest still to those that trust 'em.

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: And any wild thing grows but the more fierce and hungry for being kept up, and more dangerous to the keeper.

sp.speaker: ALITHEA
sp.p: There's doctrine for all husbands, Mr Harcourt.

sp.speaker: HARCOURT
sp.p: I edify, madam, so much, that I am impatient till I am one.

sp.speaker: DORILANT
sp.p: And I edify so much by example I will never be one.

sp.speaker: SPARKISH
sp.p: And because I will not disparage my parts, I'll ne'er be one.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: And I, alas, can't be one.

sp.speaker: PINCHWIFE
sp.p: But I must be one – against my will, to a counttry wife, with a country murrain to me.

p.seg: And I must be a country wife still too I find, for I can't, like a city one, be rid of my musty husband and do what I list.

sp.speaker: HORNER
sp.p: Now sir, I must pronounce your wife innocent, though I blush whilst I do it, and I am the only man by her now exposed to shame, which I will straight drown in wine, as you shall your suspicion; and the ladies' troubles we'll divert with a ballet. Doctor, where are your maskers?

sp.speaker: LUCY
sp.p: Indeed she's innocent, sir, I am her witness; and her end of coming out was but to see her sister's wedding, and what she has said to your face of her love to Mr Horner was but the usual innocent revenge on a husband's jealousy. Was it not, madam? Speak –

sp.speaker: MRS PINCHWIFE
sp.p: [aside to Lucy and Horner] Since you'll have me tell more lies – yes indeed, bud.

lg.l: For my own sake fain I would all believe.
Cuckolds, like lovers, should themselves deceive.
But [sighs] – his honour is least safe (too late I find)
Who trusts it with a foolish wife or friend.
Vain fops but court, and dress, and keep a pother,
To pass for women's men with one another;
But he who aims by women to be prized,
First by the men, you see, must be despised.
Now you the vigorous, who daily here
O'er vizard-mask, in public domineer,
And what you'd do to her if in place where;
Nay, have the confidence to cry, 'Come out!'
Yet when she says, 'Lead on', you are not stout,
But to your well-dressed brother straight turn round
And cry, 'Pox on her, Ned, she can't be found!'
Then slink away, a fresh one to ingage,
With so much seeming heat and loving rage,
You'd frighten listening actress on the stage;
Till she at last has seen you huffing come,
And talk of keeping in the living-room,
Yet cannot be provoked to lead her home.
Next, you Falstaffs of fifty, who beset
Your buckram maidenheads, which your friends get;
And whilst to them, you of achievements boast,
They share the booty, and laugh at your cost.
In fine, you essenc't boys, both old and young,
Who would be thought so eager, brisk, and strong,
Yet do the ladies, not their husbands, wrong;
Whose purses for your manhood make excuse,
And keep your Flanders mares for shew, not use;
Encouraged by our woman's man today,
A Horner's part may vainly think to play,
And may intrigues so bashfully disown
That they may doubted be by few or none;
May kiss the cards at picquet, hombre, loo,
And so be thought to kiss the lady too.
But gallants, have a care, faith, what you do.
The world, which to no man his due will give,
You by experience know you can deceive,
And men may still believe you vigorous,
But then, we women – there's no coz'ning us.
